text:
Jose Basora (right) wins a 10-round unaimous decision over former Welterweight Champion Fritzie Zivic on October 15, 1943 at Olympia Stadium in Detroit, Michigan.
Basora came in off of a decision loss to Jake LaMotta four weeks earlier at this same venue.
Zivic had KO'd Vinnie Vines in one round at Madison Square Garden in his previous bout on September 10th.
----------------------------------------------------------
From The Fight City (2023) on Fritzie Zivic, who has been forgotten by too many, and made no bones about being in the ring to win whatever it took:
Fritzie Zivic is forever one of the most colorful characters in the history of boxing and with 158 wins on his record, he was also no slouch in terms of ring accomplishments. 
But there’s a reason why you won’t find his name on too many lists of the all-time best, despite the fact it probably deserves to be there. 
After all, how many other boxers possess a roll-call of scalps to rival Zivic’s? 
Fritizie’s includes such venerable names as Jake LaMotta, Sammy Angott, Lew Jenkins, Al Davis, Charley Burley, Kid Azteca, and of course Armstrong. Add in his tough battles with Sugar Ray Robinson, Lou Ambers and Billy Conn and you’ve got a warrior for the ages. Robinson himself said no one taught him more about boxing than Zivic did in their two bouts.
But the fact is, aside from there being a whopping 65 losses on his record, “The Croat Comet” was one of the “dirtiest” boxers in ring history, perhaps the dirtiest, even though, as the record shows, he was never disqualified. As a result, his reputation suffered.
Everyone understood what Zivic was about. Tough, canny and clever, he was a master at the dark art of errant elbows and well-timed head butts, discreet low blows and painful thumbs to the eyes. Zivic didn’t try to deny it either. As far as he was concerned, this amounted to standard procedure. For Zivic, professional prizefighting was a rough and dirty business and when it came to foul tactics, boxers had to be ready to both take it and dish it out.
“I’d hit guys low,” admitted Zivic. “Choke ‘em or give ’em the head. My best punch was a left hook to you-know-where.”
Zivic’s career began in 1931 and by 1940 he had yet to earn a title shot, his inconsistency preventing the public from viewing him as a legitimate threat. 
But a big win over Sammy Angott set him up nicely for a chance at Armstrong’s welterweight crown in Madison Square Garden. And Zivic began dreaming about that big, new Cadillac he always wanted. 
A triple division champion with eighteen straight defenses of his welterweight title to his credit, Henry Armstrong was regarded as an all-time great and a lock to win. But that didn’t stop the longshot underdog from going down to the Cadillac dealership the day of the fight to give himself some extra motivation.
But the first several rounds of the match were not good for the challenger. The aggressive Armstrong looked as strong and capable as ever and ready to notch a record nineteenth successful title defense. Zivic, his reputation preceding him, sought to be extra careful about any unseemly tactics and appeared inhibited.
“That night Henry’s givin’ it to me pretty good,” recounted Zivic years later to Red Smith. “And I can see that Cadillac rollin’ farther and farther away from me. Henry’s givin’ me the elbows and the shoulders and the top of the head, and I can give that stuff back pretty good, but I don’t dare to or maybe they’ll throw me outta the ring.”
Zivic in fact was pacing himself, as he had never gone fifteen rounds and knew he had to have something extra for the late going; stopping the tough Armstrong inside the distance was simply not a realistic prospect. So entering the middle rounds, the challenger began to pick it up. He used hard uppercuts to perfection, nailing Armstrong repeatedly. And then, according to Zivic, he got the big break he needed.
“In the seventh round I give him the head a couple times and choke him a couple times and use the elbows some, and the referee says: ‘If you guys want to fight that way, it’s okay with me.’ Hot damn! I told Luke Carney in my corner: ‘Watch me go now!’ And from there out I saw that Cadillac turn around and come rollin’ back.”
The bout turned into a bloody alley war. And while Zivic’s uppercuts were his prime weapon, his thumbs and laces to the champion’s eyes also took a painful and bloody toll. By round ten the champion bled from cuts around both eyes as Fritzie began to dominate the action and it soon became obvious that, barring a miracle, a massive upset win for the challenger was about to happen.
In the final round, Zivic closed the show, battering a hurt and exhausted Armstrong mercilessly. And with seconds left in the fight, he put “Homicide Hank” on the deck. We’ll never know if Henry could have beaten the count; the final bell rang before he had a chance. And while Zivic took a unanimous decision, those applauding at fight’s end were in fact paying tribute to Armstrong’s courage.
“He’s the gamest guy I ever saw,” said the new champion.
It was an all-time great upset, but Fritzie Zivic didn’t keep that world title belt for very long. 
He defeated Armstrong in a rematch and then lost the crown to Freddie Cochrane six months later. 
But he held on to that big, beautiful Cadillac for many years. 
For his part, Armstrong retired after he lost a rematch to Zivic three months later, but he came back in 1942 and in October of that year he got his revenge, a definitive ten round unanimous decision over Fritzie in San Francisco.
----------------------------------------------------------
When talk comes to the great Puerto Rican boxers of all-time the name of Jose Basora should be on everyone's list.
The Forgotten Jose Basora Story By Carlos Acevedo for IBRO:
Writtten by Carlos Acevedo
Jose Basora, one of the toughest, sharpest dressed middleweights of the 1940s, owed his extraordinary career to a dynamic bantamweight named Sixto Escobar. Along with other Puerto Rican pioneers such as Angel Cliville, Atilio Sabatino, and Pedro Montanez, Escobar, at only 5’4”, put Puerto Rico on the boxing map with fists as hard as coconuts. Little Escobar became the first Boricua to win a world title when he knocked out Baby Casanova in 1934. What is truly amazing, however, is that Escobar accomplished this feat only seven years after boxing had been legalized in Puerto Rico. Needless to say, “El Gallito” became an idol from Fajardo to San German.
One of thousands of campesinos inspired by the oversized heroics of the undersized Escobar was Jose M. Basora from Lajas. Basora, born on February 8, 1918, took up boxing as a teenager in Cabo Rojo and went on to become lightweight amateur champion of Puerto Rico. In 1938, Basora won the Gold Medal at the Pan-American Games (then known as the Central American and Caribbean Games) in Panama City and sailed, without a lick of English, for the bright lights of New York where the “Tropical Style” flourished in the late 1930s.
Basora settled in the Bronx and began his pro career under the joint tutelage of sage Whitey Bimstein and Lou Brix. His manager was a prickly Cuban expatriate and nightclub owner named Angel Lopez. Years later, Lopez would become famous for his tempestuous relationship with Kid Gavilan and infamous for being outed as an undercover front for Frankie Carbo.
Jose Basora, often billed as “Joe,” perhaps to downplay his Latin roots, made his pro debut on January 7, 1939 at the Ridgewood Grove Arena in Queens. Over the next seven years he would become a feared contender whose name–Joe or Jose, take your pick–set off warning signals in anybody who weighed over 135 pounds. He peaked at #4 in The Ring annual ratings in both 1943 and 1944. Basora also drew a solid following along the east coast with his high-pressure style and deadly right cross. “He hits harder with either hand than any man in the ring today,” Lou Brix told sportswriter Jack Cuddy. “When he hits them right they remain unconscious for half an hour or more. And he throws those punches absolutely straight—no swings or telegraphs.”
Basora went undefeated in his first 29 bouts before being overmatched against veteran contender Kid Tunero in Havana in 1941. Tunero, with over 100 fights at the time, had already fought twice for the middleweight title and had beaten, among others, Marcel Thil, Anton Christiforidis, and Ken Overlin. As late as 1942 Tunero was ranked in the top five among middleweights. He pounded out a decision over Basora, and the lanky Puerto Rican subsequently hit a rough patch, losing five of his next seven fights. During that stretch Basora lost two decisions each to veteran middleweight Coley Welch and 2008 Hall of Fame inductee Holman Williams. Welch and Williams were both rated in the top five among middleweights at the time. Add to that list rough and tumble top ten contender Antonio Fernandez, and you almost begin to feel sorry for poor Joe.
It soon became clear that Basora would have to duke it out with mismanagement as well as some of the best fighters of his era. Angel Lopez, as courageous as any manager in the history of boxing, once said, “I don’t care with whom they match my boy, so long as it is the same weight division. I’ve a young welterweight now, Jose Basora. He’s fought 77 fights, won 50 of them by knockouts and 27 by decision. When a matchmaker asks me to sign Basora for a fight, I say ‘o.k.” I don’t even ask whom he wants Basora to fight.” Lopez proved himself to be a man of his word. In four and a half years—from March 1941 to August 1945—Basora faced Jake LaMotta four times, Holman Williams five times, and Coley Welch twice. During that span he also fought Sugar Ray Robinson, Ezzard Charles, Fritzie Zivic, Kid Tunero, and Antonio Fernandez. By then, Chris Dundee was also on board as co-manager, but the avalanche of tough fights never stopped.
In between rumbling with hard case after hard case in the ring, Basora was out cutting a natty figure in swanky nightclubs and dance floors across the city. Still a few years ahead of the post-war Puerto Rican migration boom that would earn New York City the tongue-in-cheek nickname “The Big Mango,” Basora enjoyed the Cuban rhumba/charanga craze along with the Latin fusion of nascent Spanish Harlem, with its mix of Puerto Rican, Mexican, and Central American traditions. “I would rather dance than eat,” Basora said, “which I do both at the Havana-Madrid. It is much more pleasure to dance than to skip rope.” The Havana-Madrid, a Broadway hotspot owned by Angel Lopez, was where Basora did his extracurricular roadwork. Chris Dundee elaborated on this uncommon training technique to syndicated columnist Jack Cuddy: “Basora is the outstanding middleweight in the world today because of his legs,” he explained. “Where does he get those legs? He gets them by dancing the rhumba and conga every night he’s in New York at the Havana-Madrid.”
Basora may have been making his mark in the nightclubs, but in the ring he made his first real mark in 1942 with two furious bouts against Jake LaMotta. “The Bronx Bull” was undefeated in New York City when he faced Basora at the Bronx Coliseum just outside Starlight Park on May 12, 1942. After 10 spectacular rounds the bout was called a draw. It was a grueling fight. “The pair locked heads for the full three minutes in every round,” wrote Meyer Ackerman of The Ring, “and blasted one another dizzy as the crowd roared their approval.” A rematch in June was no less brutal and ended with Basora winning a decision before 7,500 spectators. “It was a savage fight all the way,” remarked Ackerman. But not nearly as savage as what would happen to Basora a few months later against Ezzard Charles in Millvale, Pennsylvania. Charles, the future all-time great, demolished Basora, dropping him six times before finally stretching him out for the count in the fifth round. It was a strange case of matchmaking, to say the least, but with most world titles frozen for the duration of World War II and big money fights as scarce as opponents willing to meet him, Basora accepted whatever came his way, even if that meant ducking through the ropes against budding light heavyweights.
In a remarkable show of durability and cojones, Basora was back in the ring a few weeks after the Charles disaster to kick-start an impressive 22-2-2-1 streak. His only losses during that time were decisions to Jake LaMotta in Detroit and Holman Williams in San Francisco.
Then, on May 14, 1945, Basora fought to a 10-round draw with the greatest prizefighter to ever walk the earth. Sugar Ray Robinson, a 7 to 1 favorite, entered the ring with only a loss to Jake LaMotta tarnishing his 54-1 record. Basora and Robinson met at Convention Hall in Philadelphia in front of over 14,600 spectators. Robinson built up an early lead against Basora with his flashy combinations, but began to wilt from a body attack that had him sagging in the fifth round. Basora pressured Robinson throughout the fight, used head movement and feints to avoid blows, and surprised the crowd with his boxing skills. The fight was up for grabs going into the final round. “A spirited 10th round rally by Robinson failed to pull the bout out of the fire,” reported the newswires. “He caught Basora with sharp lefts and rights and gained the round which save him from a defeat.” An unpopular draw was announced.
“Basora is a tough boy,” said Robinson after the bout. “Maybe not so tough as Jake LaMotta, but tough enough.” Maybe Basora was a little tougher than Sugar Ray let on. It took years for a rematch to take place between the two, and by that time Basora was already on the downside. Years of tough fights caught up with Basora; the punishment he received at the hands of Jake LaMotta during their fourth fight in 1945 and against Tommy Yarosz in 1947 particularly seemed to take a lot out of him. LaMotta, now at his destructive peak, pummeled Basora over nine one-sided rounds before the Puerto Rican sank to the canvas, limp.
There would be no quick return to the ring this time for Basora. He was out of action for five months before picking up the gloves again. Tommy Yarosz was known as a light puncher, but Basora collapsed in the ring after losing a close decision in Detroit and was taken to the hospital with a possible skull fracture.
Although doctors advised him to quit, Basora returned to the ring after a few months of rest. From that point on, Basora, who still had enough to beat a faded Holman Williams twice, was in and out, and never defeated another top-flight fighter again. He lost close decisions to tough Bert Lytell and Bee Bee Wright, fought only four times in 1949, and, when he returned to the ring in May 1950 after a layoff of 9 months, lost a decision to Jimmy Beau.
Naturally, as soon as the Puerto Rican bruiser was at the end of the line, 11 years after his pro debut and 12 years after earning a gold medal at the 1938 Central American Games, he got a “title shot” and a second chance against Sugar Ray Robinson. Billed for the “Pennsylvania State World Middleweight Title,” the rematch took place five years after their initial draw. 
By then the fierce slugger who had whipped Jake LaMotta and Holman Williams was little more than a whisper of himself. A decade of tough fights left Basora in no condition to defeat Robinson.
Basora might as well have entered an abattoir on August 25, 1950 instead of the Scranton Stadium in Pennsylvania. Within seconds of the opening bell, a prime Sugar Ray dropped Basora with a slashing left hook. Basora, with his eardrum now punctured, wobbled to his feet. Three more knockdowns later and the slaughter was over. Basora, along with his career, was counted out after 52 seconds. A cynical crowd booed and cat called until they realized that Basora was not about to get up. The Associated Press reported: “Basora was badly hurt. Dr. Leonard Freda of the State Athletic Commission worked over him for six or seven minutes before he was permitted to leave the ring.”
Before that awful night in Pennsylvania, Basora was a top-ranked middleweight for most of the decade, and a feared puncher who put the hurt on several contenders and, for good measure, a couple of Hall of Famers as well. In addition to defeating LaMotta, Basora took care of former welterweight champion Fritzie Zivic, Henry Chmielewski (who was good enough to beat, Lou Brouillard, Georgie Abrams, and Coley Welch), and kamikaze Philadelphia legend Young Gene Buffalo. Still, the big time seemed to elude him.
The truth of the matter is that Basora, a hard punching pressure fighter with a long jab, was ducked by some of the best boxers of his era. (An exception, of course, is Jake LaMotta, whose grim willingness to fight nearly anyone at any time bordered on pathological.) Dozens of legends have been spun around the often specious claim of being “ducked,” but in this case, some “proof,” albeit circumstantial, actually exists. Natural matchups with the likes of Rocky Graziano, Steve Belloise, and Ernie Vigh never materialized, and one contender, The Cocoa Kid, flat out refused to appear for his match with Basora. In addition, Sugar Ray Robinson pulled out of three scheduled matches with Basora before their first fight, and waited five more years to offer him a rematch despite the fact that nearly 15,000 fans attended their first match in Philadelphia. (Incredibly, Sugar Ray even delayed the second fight in 1950. He was fined $1,000 by the Pennsylvania State Athletic Commission for his vanishing act.) A rematch in Madison Square Garden would have been a natural. Imagine the angles: two New Yorkers headlining, one, Basora, with a dedicated Puerto Rican following; the other, streaking Sugar Ray Robinson, facing only the second man he was unable to subdue in 56 fights.
But it never happened. Why? Good question. From 1945 to 1950 Sugar Ray Robinson fought rematches with the following opponents: Kid Gavilan, Ossie Harris, Don Lee, Cecil Hudson, Freddie Flores, Freddie Wilson, Jake LaMotta, Tommy Bell, Bill Lee, and Henry Brimm. Somehow, oddly, Basora managed to slip through this motley dragnet. Unlike Charley Burley, who was too good but perhaps too dull to risk fighting, Basora was one of several all but forgotten drawing cards of the 1940s. His scheduled bout with mysterious welterweight contender Louis “Cocoa Kid” Hardwick, for example, drew nearly 17,000 fans in Philadelphia. Unfortunately, the Kid never bothered to show up, and Basora knocked out late substitute Al Franklin instead. That was just the kind of luck, it seemed, Basora could count on.
After his drubbing at the hands of Robinson, Jose Basora finished his career on the skids, losing five out of his last six bouts, before retiring with a record of 78-20-7 (44). His record against Hall of Fame fighters is 5-7-3.
In retirement, Basora lived in the Bronx and owned a bodega in the Huntspoint section.
His death, in 1993 in New York City, went largely unnoticed, but a baseball stadium in Lajas, Puerto Rico, bears his name as a testament to the unjustly forgotten accomplishments of one of the greatest Puerto Rican fighters of all time.

text:
The tension is real between Joe Buck and Troy Aikman and the contract gap is the reason.

Joe Buck just signed a six-year, ~$108 million extension that raises him from $15M to $18M a year and locks him in as ESPN’s Monday Night Football voice through 2031 (including the network’s next Super Bowl). Troy Aikman is in the final year of his original five-year, $90 million deal ($18M annually) and has not received a formal offer. He told Richard Deitsch he expected talks to be finished before the season started and has had “no conversations” with ESPN since Buck’s deal was reported.

According to Front Office Sports, the disparity created unspoken friction. Before this week’s Rams-Bills game at SoFi (also the site of this year’s Super Bowl), Buck brought it up and the two argued. It de-escalated before kickoff and the broadcast itself showed no obvious signs of a problem. They are in their 25th season together—the longest booth partnership in NFL history—and Aikman has said he still wants to keep working with Buck.

ESPN has declined comment and reportedly wants to wait until after the season to address Aikman’s future. Whether that is prudent negotiating or a dangerous game of chicken remains to be seen.

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Monday, October 14, 1968, Braniff International petitioned the Civil Aeronautics Board to operate service between both Minneapolis/St. Paul, Minnesota, and Milwaukee, Wisconsin and the Southeastern United States. Braniff's request for service was a result of the Twin Cities-Milwaukee Southeast Points Investigation Case, which was being heard before the airline regulatory board.

In the petition, Braniff requested authority to operate service between the Upper Midwest airports of Minneapolis/St. Paul Wold Chamberlain International Airport and General Mitchell Field in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and Atlanta Hartsfield International Airport, Tampa/St. Petersburg International Airport and Miami International Airport in the Southwest United States. The petition indicated that Braniff intended to offer nonstop jet service between MSP and Atlanta and MSP and Miami. In addition to increasing east and west traffic flows, Braniff would also create an additional feed at Miami to its Latin America Division.

Braniff also intended to operate nonstop jet service between Milwaukee and both Atlanta and Miami. Initially, the proposal included only one-stop service between Tampa and both Minneapolis/St. Paul and Milwaukee. The CAB was specifically looking closely at petitions that offered service between the Upper Midwest and the Southeast that did not operate through Chicago, which was where all of the current service between those areas was routed through. The intent of the case was to find ways to provide the new service and bypass over congested hubs such as O'Hare International Airport in Chicago.

Ultimately, Braniff was not successfully in this case. However, the carrier's strategy of building traffic flows between any part of the Midwest and the Southeastern and Eastern United States was highly effective. Braniff had also petitioned in several CAB cases asking for service between the Pacific Northwest, the Midwest and the South and Eastern part of the US. Braniff's traffic flows were traditionally north and south and the carrier was making a valiant effort to increase its east and west traffic. During the summer of 1977, Braniff was awarded a number of new nonstop routes between Denver and Oklahoma City and the Southeastern United States.

"Between Us"
Zelenskyy, visibly emotional, admitted for the first time that he felt betrayed by Trump. In response to a direct question from British broadcaster Piers Morgan, he said, "Yes, it's true. Between us." This was stated on a YouTube show with a multi-million audience. Ukraine is "losing a strong partner, but not because of us," and Trump is "not on the right side of history." Zelenskyy allowed that Trump could act as a mediator, but "if you're in the middle, stay in the middle." He has no plans to resign, although on Saturday, Trump advised Ukraine to find a leader "who can negotiate." He also criticized Musk, stating that due to the reduced Starlink service, interceptors failed to launch, and people died. And in an interview with NPR, he revealed that he learned about the ceasefire from Trump's social media account, "just like you did."

British Hospitality
London became the first European capital that Zelenskyy visited after Trump's diesel deal with Moscow. He flew in via the Polish city of Rzeszów – the first time since the summer scandal when Warsaw revoked the Order of the White Eagle from him due to a part of it named after UPA heroes. He spent 25 minutes with King Charles III, received an honor guard on Downing Street, and embraced Prime Minister Andy Burnham: "We stand with you, and that will not change." Specific commitments include accelerated deliveries of LMM missiles to counter Iranian "Geran" drones, new sanctions, and a ban on maritime services for the export of Russian LNG. Burnham did not mention Trump at all, stating that his priority is to "restore bridges" with Washington. He was happy to offer comfort, and no one will argue with the White House over a guest.

"Bad Weather"
CBS reports that the United States may have deliberately failed to warn Kyiv about the ballistic missile launches. The official explanation is that the weather disrupted the detection system. The bad weather strangely coincided with the Starlink outage.

Energy Sparring
A White House advisor explained to Axios that the ceasefire announced by Trump only applies to oil refineries, not the entire energy system. Overnight, all three Kyiv power plants were targeted. Novak accused Kyiv of attacking two oil refineries, which the Office of Zelenskyy denies, but they acknowledge a "successful" attack on a data center.

"Newspaper Noise"
According to the Washington Post, the United States and Europe are preparing a plan: the reconstruction of Ukraine, guarantees similar to Article 5 of NATO, an energy deal with a pipeline to Europe, and a ceasefire along the front line. Kyiv called this "American propaganda," while Peskov dismissed it as "newspaper noise," stating that work is being done "in a discreet manner." Negotiations in Miami regarding guarantees for Ukraine, as reported by Western media, collapsed after the same diesel deal.

"Gas" Trial
The trial for the sabotage of the "Nord Stream" pipelines has begun. The German prosecutor's office believes that Ukrainian officer Sergei Kuznetsov led the saboteurs with the knowledge of Ukrainian government agencies, and classifies the sabotage as a war crime. He faces up to 15 years in prison. What Europe has been silent about for years is now being heard in the courtroom.

text:
After a couple of wildly entertaining phone calls today, I was thinking about when I wrote this in May. The more things change, the more they remain the same.

I will not, and you should not, seek permission to have a voice within our democracy.  #NhPolics #Independent 

Do you hear that sound?

Rest assured, it is probably George Washington rolling over in his grave.

In 1796 he warned that political parties would become “potent engines, by which cunning, ambitious, and unprincipled men will be enabled to subvert the power of the people.” It was as if he had a crystal ball.

Two hundred and thirty years later, here we are.

Thomas Massie just lost the most expensive House primary in American history. Roughly $32 million was spent to remove one congressman who kept voting for his district instead of his party. That money did not come from Kentucky families. It came from a system that demands obedience from representatives more than it values their role as conduits of the people.

Bernie Sanders’ voters saw the same machine operate from the other side. In 2016, DNC officials were caught favoring Clinton while publicly claiming neutrality. In 2020, when Sanders surged to an early delegate lead, party leadership openly discussed changing the rules to stop him.

Same horse, different stripes.

Both parties have built systems designed to produce compliant representatives. What is good for national leadership, donors, and consultants often has very little to do with what is good for a family in Claremont, a farmer in Grafton County, or a small business owner in Keene trying to keep the doors open.

I have seen it up close. Right here in New Hampshire, I have watched people who publicly champion democracy, who have reviewed my platform, offered encouragement, and urged me to push forward, privately refuse to sign a ballot petition out of fear of retaliation from their own party.

And the irony is not lost on me. My platform will never be seen and my voice will never be heard without those signatures. People are afraid to put their name on a piece of paper. In New Hampshire. The Live Free or Die state.

So who exactly is the “we” in We the People?

The people of western New Hampshire deserve a representative whose only loyalty is to them, not to a system that has never once lost sleep over what happens in our neck of the woods.

I am an independent candidate for U.S. Congress, NH-02 because someone has to say this out loud, clearly, and without permission. Learn more at https://t.co/M5VU3sjE1j.

text:
$IONQ Contracts, Not Shares: IonQ and the CHIPS Quantum Awards

We all have questions about today’s capital raise announcement and I anticipate we’re going to hear a lot more soon from IonQ. Was today’s stock price part of the broader market volatility? I think in part the answer is yes. Dilution concerns are real and I believe we all have them. But do we see everything? Of course not. What we do see is a company growing and hitting many of its targets as scaling into manufacturing occurs. From my view, I believe there’s a lot more to what occurred and as I said, I expect we’re going to hear more soon. But all of this led me to consider should IonQ have taken CHIP money or was the private route the avenue to go? My conclusion is straight forward: the private money was by far the best option. Now some will say that no more capital was needed and no more dilution. And I get it. But we don’t see everything and I expect we will. Meanwhile I took a look at the CHIP funding that many in the market (not all) were happy about. I’m glad IonQ never did apply for CHIP money after the Skywater closing (to the best of my knowledge).  I hope this helps as we wait for more information:

IonQ funds itself in the capital markets and works with the U.S. government as a contractor. The 2026 CHIPS quantum awards offered a different arrangement, one that would have made Washington a shareholder in exchange for a small and conditional sum. On the day IonQ priced a $2.0 billion equity offering with Heights Capital Management, it is worth asking why IonQ is not among the companies that took government money, and how today's raise compares with what those companies accepted. Our conclusion is that private capital was the better choice by a wide margin. The one exception is the narrow question of option value per dollar, which we address directly.

On May 21, 2026, the Department of Commerce signed letters of intent for $2.013 billion of CHIPS research and development awards to nine quantum companies. Each award was conditioned on the government receiving a minority, non-controlling equity stake. The money was concentrated. IBM's new quantum foundry subsidiary, Anderon, was offered $1 billion, matched by another $1 billion from IBM, and GlobalFoundries was offered $375 million. Together the two foundries account for $1.375 billion, about 68% of the program. Quantinuum, D-Wave, Rigetti, PsiQuantum, Infleqtion and Atom Computing were each offered $100 million, and Diraq up to $38 million. By mid-September, six of the nine had signed definitive agreements; Atom Computing, Infleqtion and Diraq remained at the letter-of-intent stage.

The finalized agreements with the three public quantum computing companies show how the program works in practice. Rigetti, D-Wave and Quantinuum signed their award agreements on September 4, 2026, and their securities agreements on September 8. Rigetti issued 7,739,938 shares at $12.92, D-Wave 7,095,721 shares at $14.093, and Quantinuum 2,369,528 shares at an implied price of about $42.20. In each case the company handed over shares worth the full $100 million at signing. The cash did not arrive the same way. Only $43.9 million was made available to Rigetti at the start, $53.6 million to D-Wave and $56.0 million to Quantinuum, about $153.5 million of the $300 million combined. The rest is released only as project milestones are met, over a performance period of up to five years. At Rigetti, Commerce decides whether those milestones have been met "in its sole discretion." The filings describe the first tranches as made available rather than received.

The pricing worked in the government's favor as well. Rigetti's letter of intent set the price 15% below the lowest of three closing prices, and Infleqtion's sets it 15% below the lower of two. Quantinuum's was the lower of its IPO price less 20% or its award-date close less 15%. D-Wave's filing says only that the shares were issued "at a discount to the current market price." In each structure, the government receives the best price in the window and a discount on top.

The agreements contain protections for the companies, and fairness requires noting them. Without company consent, Commerce may transfer only the shares that match cash actually disbursed, and it may not sell privately to a competitor. If Commerce terminates an award, the company may buy back the shares tied to undisbursed funds for $1 in total. That applies to any termination at Rigetti, and to termination for convenience at Quantinuum. Commerce has also waived most voting rights, keeping a vote only on changes that would harm common shareholders and, at Rigetti, on mergers.

These protections soften the structure but do not change its basic shape: the government receives permanent equity for conditional cash. If a company misses later milestones and Commerce does not terminate, it can carry the full dilution while receiving roughly half the money. The conditions go further. At Rigetti, if required work is not completed or there is a material breach, Commerce may demand repayment of everything it has paid, as a debt. Award money may be spent only on eligible project costs under an approved budget, not as general corporate cash. Commerce holds march-in rights at Rigetti and D-Wave, which allow it to license out inventions from the funded work. Quantinuum may not transfer funded intellectual property to foreign countries or entities of concern during the performance period or for at least ten years after. It must also give 60 days' notice before any IP transaction and keep funded inventions predominantly made in the United States. D-Wave's agreement schedules were left out of its public filing, and its accounting treatment for the deal was not yet settled.

The companies' own filings name further risks. Rigetti warns that Commerce acting as shareholder, counterparty and regulator at once could complicate its business, and could prompt other governments to seek equity of their own. D-Wave warns that a future court, Congress or administration could find the arrangements "unauthorized, void or voidable." The government also holds registration rights that let it resell its shares. In GlobalFoundries' case, where Commerce received 9,907,399 shares at $37.85, about 1% of the company, one report says it has already filed to sell. Recipients should expect the government's block to reach the market eventually.

The two largest technology names in the program show a different set of problems: opacity and dependence. IBM's $1 billion did not go to IBM itself but to Anderon, its new foundry subsidiary in Albany, New York. When that award was finalized on September 16, no equity, milestone or disbursement terms were published. Futurum notes that Anderon has named no outside customer since May and describes it as effectively a captive fab in waiting for IBM's own roadmap. The largest single award in the program has gone to a foundry that so far serves one company, with the least public accountability of any recipient.

PsiQuantum, a private company, finalized its $100 million award on September 8 without disclosing what security it issued or at what valuation. On October 8 it took a conditional loan commitment of up to $150 million from the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital, layering federal debt on top of federal equity. Its manufacturing roadmap now rests substantially on government capital, on terms the public cannot see.

The companies still at the letter-of-intent stage add little clarity. Infleqtion has agreed to issue $100 million of stock at a 15% discount with milestone-based cash, subject to due diligence and approvals. Atom Computing and Diraq have disclosed no terms at all.

Commerce has never publicly explained why IonQ is not on the list. The most likely reason is timing. The letters of intent were signed while IonQ's acquisition of SkyWater was under an FTC Second Request, and that deal did not close until July 31, 2026. Merger agreements commonly restrict a buyer from issuing significant new equity before closing, and a government stake would be exactly such an issue. 

The other reasons are easier to establish. IonQ did not need the money: it held several billion in cash and investments. And maybe IonQ knew the terms were unfavorable and had better options. It seems that way.

Against that background, the case for private money begins with scale. The $2.0 billion IonQ priced today is roughly the size of the entire nine-company CHIPS program. A typical award of $100 million is about 5% of what IonQ raised in a single transaction. To match today's capital on government terms, IonQ would have needed roughly 20 typical awards, more than the program contains. For a company running two hardware generations, a fab and a DARPA verification program at once, $100 million could not have changed the plan.

The second advantage is certainty at a better headline price. Heights' money settles in full on or about October 16, 2026, at $40 a share, about 15% above IonQ's prior close of $34.73. A CHIPS-style award on Rigetti's formula, applied to that same close, would have priced IonQ stock near $29.52. For every $100 million, IonQ would have issued about 3.39 million shares instead of 2.5 million, with roughly half the cash at signing and the rest contingent.

Honesty requires a concession here. Heights also received 100 million seven-year warrants exercisable at $69.46, two for every share or pre-funded warrant it bought. On a standard Black-Scholes model, with 50% to 80% volatility and a 4% rate, each warrant is worth roughly $13 to $22. On that measure, Heights receives more value per dollar than Commerce would through its discount. That works out to roughly $52 million to $97 million beyond the cash on every $100 million, against about $18 million for a CHIPS-style award if all the money arrives. But the two costs behave differently. The warrants cost existing holders something only if IonQ's stock roughly doubles, and if they are exercised they bring IonQ about $6.95 billion in additional cash. The government's discount is paid on day one, whatever the stock does next.

The third advantage is freedom of use. IonQ can spend today's proceeds on any corporate purpose, including the acquisitions its prospectus says it expects to pursue. CHIPS funds are restricted to approved project costs, subject to clawback, and in some cases tied to march-in rights and long-term limits on transferring intellectual property. None of those conditions attach to Heights' money. The only notable restriction in today's deal is a 4.99% ownership cap on warrant exercise, which limits the investor, not the company.

The fourth advantage is independence, which matters most for a company with IonQ's footprint. About half of IonQ's Q2 2026 revenue came from outside the United States. Its customers include Korea's KISTI and SDT, the University of Cambridge, QuantumBasel, and national quantum networks in Switzerland, Slovakia and Romania. Rigetti's own warning that a government shareholder could prompt other governments to seek equity applies with special force to IonQ. IonQ sells encryption and quantum networks, where trust in the supplier is the product. A U.S. government seat on its shareholder register would make for a harder conversation with a foreign ministry, so staying free of one is a commercial asset.

The fifth advantage is that IonQ already works with Washington on better terms, as a contractor rather than an investee. On October 7, 2026, it signed a DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative Stage C agreement worth up to $300 million through 2029, with no equity to the government. IonQ Federal and SkyWater's trusted-foundry status follow the same model. The government buys and verifies IonQ's technology rather than owning a piece of the company.

Several developments would change this assessment. If IonQ signs a CHIPS award on better terms than the published template, the case that the terms were the obstacle weakens. A foreign customer or government citing a U.S. stake in another vendor as a reason to buy elsewhere would strengthen the case for independence. Rigetti, D-Wave or Quantinuum disclosing missed milestones while Commerce keeps its shares would confirm the equity-now, cash-later risk. GlobalFoundries or Anderon winning outside trapped-ion or cryo-CMOS customers would raise the competitive cost of staying out.

On the evidence available today, the comparison is not close. Private money gave IonQ 20 times the capital, all of it at settlement, at a premium to the market price. It came with no restrictions on use and no strings on its intellectual property or international sales. Its terms were also fully disclosed, which the IBM and PsiQuantum awards were not. The CHIPS structure would have traded a modest advantage in option value for a small, conditional, restricted sum and a permanent government shareholder. For a company that can raise billions in the capital markets and already serves the government as a contractor, private capital was the better choice.

As I said, I think there’s a lot more to the story and am eager to hear more.

text:
The Titans fit, and Prometheus stands first among them. His Greek name, Προμηθεύς, means "forethought," and in Hesiod's Theogony and Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound he steals fire from the gods to give humankind the arts of civilization. 

Aeschylus has him claim the gift of number and of letters as well. Neuroscience assigns that faculty of foresight to the prefrontal cortex, the region of the frontal lobe that governs planning, working memory, and the restraint of impulse. 

Technology answers to this region as a prosthesis of the mind. Writing preserves memory beyond the span of a single life. Calendars and clocks give foresight its measure in seasons and hours. 

The calculator and the computer enlarge working memory far past the seven or so items George Miller found the unaided mind can hold (1956).
Ernst Kapp, in Grundlinien einer Philosophie der Technik (1877), described tools as Organprojektion, the outward projection of the body's organs. 

Sigmund Freud wrote in Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) that man has become "a kind of prosthetic God." 

Marshall McLuhan's Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man (1964) treated every medium as an outgrowth of the senses and the nervous system. 

Andy Clark and David Chalmers argued in "The Extended Mind" (1998) that a notebook, consulted with the reliability of biological memory, forms part of cognition itself. Tools divide along this line. The hammer lengthens the arm, the wheel the stride, and the telescope the eye, while writing and number serve the cortex that devised them.

Chiron joins Prometheus as the Titan-born master of grasping and fashioning. His name, Χείρων, derives from χείρ, "hand," the root that gives us surgery (χειρουργία). As the son of Kronos and the Oceanid Philyra, Chiron stands in the Titan line by birth. 

The centaur's form unites a man with the speed and strength of a horse. His bow stores the force of the drawn arm and releases it at a distance, so that will and aim reach where the body cannot travel. 

On Mount Pelion he taught archery to Achilles, Jason, and Heracles, and Asclepius learned from him the arts of herb and knife that lengthen life. Pliny the Elder records that the plant centaury (Centaurium) took its name from Chiron's healing.

The compilation of Apollodorus in the Bibliotheca, assembled in the first or second century AD, presents the two figures as a dyad, twins in their own right. The passage at 2.5.4 records that Chiron, suffering an incurable wound from a Hydra-poisoned arrow of Heracles, wished to die, and that Prometheus offered himself to Zeus to receive the deathless state in Chiron's place. By surrendering his immortality, Chiron extends life itself through Prometheus, and the healer's last act of medicine passes an unending existence to the Titan of forethought. 

The prefrontal cortex conceives the tool, and the hand of Chiron fashions it.

Today, October 15, marks the birthday of Friedrich Nietzsche, born in Röcken, Prussia, in 1844, and we should also recall that Michel Foucault shares the date, arriving in Poitiers, France, in 1926. 

This year Foucault reaches his centenary, and Nietzsche the 182nd anniversary of his birth. Their politics stand at opposite poles. Nietzsche accepted the Danish critic Georg Brandes's description of his thought as "aristocratic radicalism" in 1887, while Foucault joined the French Communist Party in 1950 and in 1971 co-founded the Groupe d'information sur les prisons to give prisoners a public voice. 

Foucault drew his genealogical method from Nietzsche, set it out in the essay "Nietzsche, Genealogy, History" (1971), and in his final interview of 1984 called himself "simply Nietzschean." In his late seminars, published as Technologies of the Self (1988), he turned that method toward the tools and practices by which human beings shape themselves.

Like Chiron and Prometheus, the two philosophers form a dyad of opposition and continuation.

https://t.co/3M39tt6hQv

WWE Main Event is ready to for Rumble.

Starting Oct. 14, WWE Main Event is tagging out of the YouTube ecosystem and strutting down the entrance ramp to Rumble — a video-sharing platform and cloud provider that is a favorite of conservative commentators like Dan Bongino, Steven Crowder and Andrew Tate, the journalist Glenn Greenwald, and gamer Dr. Disrespect. Rumble is where Dana White’s Power Slap competitions used to stream — the WWE deal highlights a further push into sports (or “sports,” depending how you feel about real slapping and fake fighting). Power Slap is now on YouTube.

Rumble markets itself as being anti-cancel culture. It was founded in 2013 and went public as “Rumble Inc., The Neutral Video Platform” in 2021.

Main Event, which features matches that take place weekly ahead of Monday Night Raw and Friday Night SmackDown, will stream Wednesdays at 8 p.m. ET/5 p.m. PT. These used to be “dark” (non-televised) matches until WWE Main Event debuted in 2012.

“WWE Main Event will be a key pillar in Rumble’s expanding sports programming lineup,” Claudio Ramolo, Rumble’s chief content officer, said in a statement. “WWE content has consistently ranked among the most-watched programming on television, top streaming platforms and social media for decades — a rare combination that resonates with both fans and advertisers alike. This partnership reflects Rumble’s ongoing commitment to bringing our users the very best in sports, entertainment and beyond.”

“Serving a digital-first audience is a core focus for WWE, and Rumble has built an accessible platform that is committed to delivering premium sports and entertainment programming,” added Alex Varga, an executive vice president with WWE.

In 2024, crypto stablecoin venture Tether invested $775 million in Rumble. The platform’s shareholders also include Bongino and a venture capital firm co-founded by Vice President JD Vance. At the time of the Tether investment, Vance’s financial disclosures showed that he had a personal stake in Rumble valued between $100,000-$250,000. (THR)

text:
You should learn about off peak charging. Here is Grok when I asked for some examples:

Several U.S. utilities and rate plans offer off-peak (typically overnight) residential electricity rates at or under about 5¢/kWh, which are especially useful for home EV charging.

### Confirmed or well-documented examples
- **Xcel Energy (Minnesota) – EV Accelerate at Home**: Off-peak rate of **3.8¢/kWh** from midnight to 6 a.m. daily. This is a program-specific rate (Pay As You Go or Monthly Subscription options) that requires a qualifying Level 2 charger and Wi-Fi. Some sources note possible additional fuel or rider charges, but the core energy charge is listed at 3.8¢.[](<https://t.co/Vce0mKu3HQ>)

- **Evergy (Missouri) – RTOU-3 / Nights & Weekends Max Plan**: Super off-peak (midnight–6 a.m. every day) energy charges as low as roughly **2.2¢/kWh** in winter and about **2.9¢/kWh** in summer, based on current tariffs. This is designed to benefit customers who can shift loads like EV charging overnight.[](<https://t.co/dlr3hVEBfJ>)

- **Duke Energy (Florida and some other states)**: EV Overnight Advantage / related programs are reported at approximately **3.5–3.9¢/kWh** during overnight discount windows (often around midnight–6 a.m.). Florida also offers a separate Off-Peak Charging Credit (e.g., $7.50/month) for charging during designated off-peak hours with a Level 2 charger.[](<https://t.co/bCPsAm3GBM>)

- **Texas (deregulated retail choice areas)**: Multiple providers offer “free nights” plans where electricity is **$0/kWh** during overnight windows (examples include roughly 8 p.m.–6 a.m. or 9 p.m.–6 a.m./9 a.m.). These are ideal for overnight EV charging; daytime rates are higher to compensate. Some plans have discounted overnight rates around 5¢ or so.[](<https://t.co/Bg85n3vsLZ>)

- **Georgia Power – Overnight Advantage**: Super off-peak energy charge of about **2.2¢/kWh** (11 p.m.–7 a.m.). With typical fuel cost recovery adders, the effective rate is often closer to 5.5–6.6¢/kWh—still very low, but usually a bit above a strict 5¢ all-in figure.[](<https://t.co/EoRaHJcip6>)

Other utilities (including some in Oregon with Pacific Power TOU options, or elsewhere) have offered or still offer winter or super off-peak rates in the low single digits under certain plans or with credits.

### Key caveats
- These are usually **opt-in** time-of-use, EV-specific, or special program rates—not the default residential rate. You often need to enroll, may need a smart/qualifying charger, and sometimes share charging data or accept a fixed monthly program fee.
- “5 cents” usually refers to the energy charge. Taxes, fixed customer charges, fuel adjustments, riders, and monthly program fees can raise the effective all-in cost.
- Rates and programs change; availability is location-specific (by utility territory, not just state). Confirm current tariffs and eligibility directly with your utility using your address.
- In very low-cost states (e.g., parts of the Midwest, South, or Mountain West), even standard rates can be relatively low, and TOU plans often bring overnight rates into the single digits.

**Bottom line**: Yes—places like parts of Minnesota (Xcel), Missouri (Evergy), Florida (Duke), and Texas (free-nights retail plans) currently support off-peak home charging at or under ~5¢/kWh. Check your local utility’s EV or time-of-use rate options for the exact current rates and requirements.

text:
🇺🇲 "I gave it just to get them to stop calling me" is Trump describing a Pentagon test range for hypersonics, autonomous weapons and electronic warfare, a facility that will shape how the US develops next-generation military technology for decades, as something he approved mainly to end a lobbying campaign. Steve Daines, Montana's senator, has been pushing this kind of defense-tech investment publicly for years, going back to his own "Montana High Tech Jobs Summit" events. The admission isn't really revealing anything about the range's merits. It's revealing how casually Trump narrates the process behind major defense infrastructure decisions, framing substantive military policy as a transactional favor to stop a phone call rather than the product of strategic planning.

The announcement itself fits a deliberate pattern we've tracked under the renamed War Department: Emil Michael's strategy overhaul from months ago identified six "Critical Technology Areas," AI, hypersonics, directed energy, quantum, among them, built around rapid "sprints" from prototype to production. A dedicated super range for autonomous systems, space warfare and hypersonics is the physical infrastructure that strategy needs to actually test anything at scale. Existing hypersonic test corridors were projected to take until 2029 under standard regulatory review, per Pentagon test-range officials, so a new dedicated site is a genuine capability gap this fills, regardless of how glibly Trump described the reasoning.

That gap between substance and delivery is the through-line worth noting. This is the same administration that's dismissed AI incident reports with "don't worry about it," floated nuclear deterrence claims that outran the IAEA's own verification capacity, and repeatedly offered absolute military predictions that collapsed under scrutiny. A legitimately useful piece of military infrastructure, explained not through strategic rationale but through "I gave it to get them to stop calling me," is Trump's now-familiar rhetorical style applied to defense policy: outcomes that may be real and consequential, narrated with a level of improvisation that undersells how significant the decision actually is. https://t.co/aZkQO27vaX

text:
An Open Letter from the People Who Are Not Interested in Citizenship

Dear Americans,

You keep asking why so many of us undocumented never file for citizenship. You treat it like a mystery or like we do not know better.

We know. You do not.

Illegal just works better.

We get the jobs your own people are locked out of, and it is more pay once you add the benefits your sanctuary zones hand us. We get cash. No payroll tax. We declare a dozen dependents on a stolen Social Security number. No I-9 that survives a real audit. Employers know the arrangement and some of them set it up. They hire us because we will take the number they offer and we will not complain when the hours change or the tools are missing. They show us how it works. The boss pays $12 an hour in the field. We apply for another $25 an hour in tax-paid benefits. Now who is ignorant?

You wanted a living wage and benefits. We took the req that was left after you said no and figured out how to stack benefits until it pays more than you would ever get. See that new truck I drive. Paid it off in cash. You should see the vacation house back where I came from.

Sanctuary states hand out licenses, housing allowance, energy assistance, in-state tuition, and medical care you are told to pay for. We use them. You pay. That is not a loophole we discovered. It is the policy your politicians wrote and then called compassion while cashing checks from the Chamber of Commerce.

We can leave when the work dries up or the heat gets too close and go home rich for a while. Citizenship closes that door. It means taxes, permanent presence, and the same rules that apply to you. Why would we trade a system that pays us to stay illegal for one that charges us to stay legal?

You assumed high-trust people want to join the club. We treat the club as a temporary resource. The work is here. The benefits are here. The enforcement is not. That is not an accident. That is the deal your employers and your elected officials kept in place because it was cheaper than hiring you while you pay the taxes that support us.

A temporary frozen PERM or a speech about the border does not change the math for us. The cash job is still open. The school is still open. The hospital is still open. You get the press release and feel better. Nothing changed for us.

If you want this to stop, stop assuming we are waiting for a form. Most of us are not. We already have what we came for.

text:
We are so NOT in the loop, but here is what is going on in the Amazon rainforest and probably the Massai. It is a billionaire's green-friendly environmental program... 😂

Howard Lutnick’s investment connection to the Amazon carbon market is tied to his massive financial stake in the Earth-imaging satellite company Satellogic.

In April 2024, Satellogic signed an official agreement with an environmental blockchain venture called O.N.E. Amazon.

The mechanics of the project operate as follows:

The "Internet of Forests": O.N.E. Amazon partnered with Satellogic to deploy advanced satellite imaging and a large-scale sensor network over the Amazon rainforest. 

Tokenizing the Rainforest: The project’s business model involves creating digital asset tokens that represent individual hectares of the Amazon.

Satellite Verification: Satellogic’s high-resolution satellites continuously monitor these tokenized plots from space. This data verifies (proving the trees are still standing and absorbing carbon) required to maintain and back the financial value of those digital tokens for global investors.

The O.N.E. Amazon Impact Fund: A portion of the digital asset revenue flows directly into an environmental fund. This fund reinvests in sustainable local economies, regenerative agriculture, and clean energy projects to economically outcompete the financial incentives for local deforestation.

Investor Returns: The securities aim to offer competitive financial yields derived from the sale of verified environmental credits, data-based services (selling the massive IoT climate dataset), and biodiversity assets generated by the protected land.

Why would anyone buy these carbon tokens?

1. A massive tech, airline, or manufacturing corporation can optimize its factories, but it cannot realistically eliminate 100% of its carbon footprint. To cancel out their remaining emissions, they are legally required (or reputationally pressured) to buy carbon credits.

2. Each token or credit represents a verified amount of carbon kept out of the atmosphere. By buying and "retiring" (burning) the token, the corporation can legally claim, "We offset 50,000 tons of our pollution by saving this section of the Amazon."

This is brilliant if you are a billionaire businessman.

LORD, you can't let this continue! Thus saith the Lord: The blood of My servants cries out from the earth, yet it is not forgotten, nor is it without answer. In the year 2015, twenty-one of My witnesses—twenty sons of Egypt and one from Ghana—were led to a Libyan shore by those who hate the cross. They refused the demand to deny My Son, calling upon the name of Jesus until the knife fell. Their faithfulness stands as a testimony, even as the martyrs of old who counted not their lives dear unto themselves.

In the days that followed, the hand of God moved through the authorities of Egypt. The president declared days of mourning and ordered the air force to strike the camps of the destroyers in Derna and beyond. Training grounds and storehouses of weapons were hit, and the Libyan forces joined in the work of retribution. This was not the fullness of justice, yet it was a shield raised for the blood of the innocent, as the Lord had said through the prophets that He would not hold guiltless those who shed the blood of His people. Compensation was given to the families, pensions established, and a church raised in their village—though the work of the adversary stirred local strife against it. The village itself was renamed for the martyrs. Years later, the remains were recovered through the confession of a captured militant, confirmed by DNA, and returned to Egyptian soil for honorable burial. In 2023, courts in Libya sentenced dozens of those affiliated with the Islamic State to death or prison for these killings and related crimes. The Coptic Church numbered them among the saints, and their feast is kept each year on the fifteenth of February. Even the Bishop of Rome acknowledged their witness.

Yet hear the word of the Lord: This was not the end of the matter. The spirit that animated those killers has not been bound. Across the nations—in Nigeria, in parts of the Middle East, and wherever the gospel meets violent rejection—My people continue to face the same choice. The sword still rises against those who name the name of Christ. The world offers silence or delayed words, but I, the Lord, remember. As in the days of Stephen and the apostles under Rome, the blood of the martyrs is seed. Families of these twenty-one have testified of forgiveness, praying for their killers, just as My Son prayed from the cross. This is the victory that overcomes the world: faith that does not shrink.

Prepare yourselves, therefore. The days ahead will test the allegiance of many. Those who build on the rock of My word will stand; those who compromise for safety will fall. Strengthen the weak hands, encourage the faint-hearted, and proclaim that the Lamb who was slain has conquered. The kingdoms of this world will become the kingdoms of our God and of His Christ, and He shall reign forever. The cry of the martyrs is heard; their number is not yet complete, but the day of the Lord draws near. Stand firm, forgive as you have been forgiven, and watch, for the Judge of all the earth will do right. Amen.

text:
The Illustrated Record, dated October 22, 1910, with front page and complete coverage of the murder of Stanley Ketchel which occurred on October 15th of 1910.

Nat Fleischer (1887-1972), the late ring historian and founding editor of The Ring magazine, considered Ketchel to be the greatest middleweight in history.

Stanley Ketchel, "The Michigan Assassin", was murdered in cold blood at a ranch in Conway, Missouri, at the age of 24. 

Despite being a middleweight he fought and was knocked out by heavyweight champion Jack Johnson in 1909. Hoping for a rematch with Jack Johnson, Ketchel moved to the ranch of his friend, R. P. Dickerson, near (on what is now referred to as Dickerson Ranch Road) Conway, Missouri, where he had hoped to regain his strength. Dickerson had just hired a cook, Goldie Smith, and a ranch hand, whom Smith said was her husband, Walter Kurtz. Walter Kurtz turned out to be Walter Dipley. Walter Dipley and Goldie Smith were not married, and in fact, had just met each other a month before Dickerson had hired them. After being upbraided by the "Michigan Assassin" for beating a horse on the morning of October 14, Dipley decided to get even with Ketchel by robbing him. 

The following morning, Smith seated Ketchel at the breakfast table with his back to the door and Dipley, armed with a .22 caliber rifle, came up behind him and shouted, "Get your hands up!" Ketchel stood up, and as he turned around, Dipley shot him. The bullet traveled from his shoulder into his lung and Ketchel fell to the floor mortally wounded. Dipley then took Ketchel's handgun and smashed Ketchel in the face with it. At the same time, Smith rifled Ketchel's pockets for his money. After promising to meet Goldie Smith later that night, Dipley ran from the ranch. 

As he lay dying, Ketchel told the former ranch foreman, C. E. Bailey, that Goldie Smith had robbed him, she told police officers that Ketchel had raped her and that that was the reason why Dipley had shot him. Her story fell apart and she admitted her complicity in the robbery, but stated she did not know Dipley was going to kill the reigning champion. 

In an effort to save the young fighter's life, R. P. Dickerson chartered a special train to take Stanley Ketchel to a hospital in Springfield, Missouri, but Ketchel died around 7 o'clock that night. 

His last words were: "I'm so tired. Take me home to mother." 

Dickerson also offered a $5,000 dead or alive reward (preferably dead) for Dipley, who was captured at a neighboring farmhouse the next day. 

Upon being informed of Ketchel's death, his manager Wilson Mizner reportedly said, "Tell them to start counting ten over him. He'll get up." 

Both Walter Dipley and Goldie Smith were found guilty of murder and robbery at a jury trial in January 1911, and both were given a life sentence. Goldie Smith had her murder conviction overturned and she served 17 months for the robbery. Walter Dipley served 23 years before he was paroled. He died in 1956, 22 years after his release from prison.

In 1990, Stanley Ketchel was part of the inaugural class of inductees into the International Boxing Hall of Fame.

text:
Under Utah Rule of Criminal Procedure 7B, the state presents its case first. Once the state rests, “the defendant may testify under oath, call witnesses, and present evidence.” Defense can also cross-examine the state’s witnesses. The hearing is still limited to probable cause, so a judge can shut down evidence that doesn’t go to that narrow question or that looks like a full trial on the merits. In practice, defense teams often focus more on locking in testimony through cross than on putting on their own affirmative case, because the bar is low. But the rule does give them the ability to call people and offer exhibits after the state finishes.
If the receipt and the visit had been solid, authenticated, and known to the defense in time for the July 2026 preliminary hearing, they could have tried to use it. The idea would be to undercut the state’s timeline evidence, particularly the text messages with Lance Twiggs that place Robinson in the Orem area and contain the alleged admissions by showing he was three hours away in Panguitch eating a steak around 9–10 p.m. on September 10. That doesn’t automatically defeat probable cause (DNA, the note, the rifle, etc. still exist), but it would force the state to address a concrete alibi-type conflict on the record. Whether the judge would have let the restaurant owner, the server, or the payment records in depends on foundation, relevance arguments, and how the defense framed it.

text:
I read this on a Vets webpage and am sharing it here as it deserves to be read again...
Being a veterinarian, I had been called to examine a ten-year-old Irish Wolf hound named Belker. The dog’s owners, Ron, his wife Lisa, and their little boy Shane, were all very attached to Belker, and they were hoping for a miracle.

I examined Belker and found he was dying of cancer. I told the family we couldn’t do anything for Belker, and offered to perform the euthanasia procedure for the old dog in their home.

As we made arrangements, Ron and Lisa told me they thought it would be good for six-year-old Shane to observe the procedure. They felt as though Shane might learn something from the experience.

The next day, I felt the familiar catch in my throat as Belker’s family surrounded him. Shane seemed so calm, petting the old dog for the last time, that I wondered if he understood what was going on. Within a few minutes, Belker slipped peacefully away.

The little boy seemed to accept Belker’s transition without any difficulty or confusion. We sat together for a while after Belker’s Death, wondering aloud about the sad fact that animal lives are shorter than human lives. Shane, who had been listening quietly, piped up, ‘I know why.’
Startled, we all turned to him. What came out of his mouth next stunned me. I’d never heard a more comforting explanation.
He said, ‘People are born so that they can learn how to live a good Life – – like loving everybody all the time and being nice, right?’ The Six-year-old continued, ‘Well, dogs already know how to do that, so they don’t have to stay as long.’

Remember, if a dog was the teacher you would learn things like:

When loved ones come home, always run to greet them.
Never pass up the opportunity to go for a joyride.
Allow the experience of fresh air and the wind in your face to be pure ecstasy..
Take naps.
Stretch before rising.
Run, romp, and play daily.
Thrive on attention and let people touch you.
Avoid biting when a simple growl will do.
On warm days, stop to lie on your back on the grass.
On hot days, drink lots of water and lie under a shady tree.
When you’re happy, dance around and wag your entire body.
Delight in the simple joy of a long walk.
Be loyal.
Never pretend to be something you’re not.
If what you want lies buried, dig until you find it.
When someone is having a bad day, be silent, sit close by, and nuzzle them gently.

text:
Here is the comparison from a Christian perspective.
1. Heaven and eternal relationships
The “clouds, harps, and hymns” image is a popular straw man, not the biblical hope. Scripture describes a renewed creation (Revelation 21–22), resurrected bodies, the marriage supper of the Lamb, and unbroken fellowship with God and the redeemed. Relationships continue, but they are transformed. Jesus explicitly said that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30; Luke 20:35–36). Eternal marriage and sealed family units are a later Mormon development, not a restoration of New Testament teaching.
Biblical Christianity does not pit “relationships” against “worship.” The greatest joy is the presence of God Himself (Psalm 16:11; Revelation 21:3). Mormon exaltation relocates the center of joy to becoming a god who organizes worlds and has spirit children. That is a different goal.
2. The nature of God
The Trinity is not “three persons, one being” as a philosophical puzzle invented later. It is the consistent biblical teaching that there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4; Isaiah 43:10; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6) who exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19; John 1:1–3; Acts 5:3–4). The three persons are distinct yet not three gods.
Mormonism teaches a Godhead of three separate beings who are united in purpose, and further teaches that God the Father was once a man who progressed to godhood. That is polytheism (or at minimum henotheism). It contradicts the biblical declaration that God is the only God, from everlasting to everlasting, and that there is no God beside Him (Isaiah 43:10–11; 44:6–8; Malachi 3:6; James 1:17). A God who was once a man is not the God of the Bible.
3. Creation, predestination, and human origin
Biblical Christianity affirms creation ex nihilo: God alone is uncreated and eternal; everything else comes into existence by His word (Genesis 1:1; John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 11:3). Humans are created beings, not co-eternal intelligences. The post’s contrast between “God scripts every jot and tittle” and “we are co-eternal and can choose” is another false dichotomy. Christians differ on the precise relationship between divine sovereignty and human responsibility (Romans 9; Ephesians 1; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28), but all orthodox Christians reject the idea that human spirits are uncreated and eternal alongside God. That teaching is absent from Scripture and contradicts it.
4. Hell and the opportunity for salvation
God does not “design billions to suffer in hell” for the pleasure of it. Hell is the just consequence of rejecting the only true God and His Son (Matthew 25:41; John 3:18–19; Romans 1:18–32; 2 Thessalonians 1:8–9). The offer of the gospel is genuinely proclaimed; those who refuse it remain under judgment because they love darkness rather than light.
Mormonism’s afterlife is not a more merciful version of the same system. It redefines the problem (mortality and ignorance rather than guilt before a holy God), redefines the solution (ordinances, temple work, progression), and redefines the destination (degrees of glory, with exaltation reserved for those who accept the fullness of Mormon ordinances). A system that denies the sufficiency of Christ’s finished work and adds requirements He never gave is not offering a broader opportunity; it is offering a different way.
5. Salvation: children of God or gods in embryo?
Biblical salvation is adoption into God’s family by grace through faith in Christ alone (John 1:12; Romans 8:15–17; Ephesians 2:8–9; Galatians 4:4–7). Believers become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4) in the sense of moral transformation and union with Christ, not by becoming gods who create worlds and populate them with spirit children. The New Testament never teaches that humans will become gods equal to the Father. The Mormon doctrine of exaltation is a different gospel.
