MACRO:

Anthropic’s revenue climbed 45% to $16.8 billion in the third quarter, according to WSJ sources ahead of its IPO next month. The Co. did not disclose its much anticipated ARR number for Sept-end but analysts deduced it to be much lower than many had hoped, with revenue growth slowing. Nonetheless, Reuters cited analysts who met with the Co. who suggested Anthropic could still see its annual revenue run rate reach $110 billion by the end of the year. (WSJ, RTRS, BBG)

A deepening sell-off in semiconductor groups rattled global equity markets on Thursday, as mounting concerns over inflation and the future earnings of AI groups hit stocks and pushed investors into haven assets. Kospi fell by 8 per cent, the Nikkei 225 sank 5.3 per cent. Bond markets rallied in a sign that investors were moving into less risky assets. (FT)

The cost of insuring against US tech defaults has hit record levels in the latest sign of credit stress building in the AI trade, especially for data centres dependent on future revenue. (RTRS)

'Investor appetite for data centre IPOs is reaching its limit' FT article highlights three major deals that have recently stumbled: Blackstone-backed AirTrunk postponed its $1.5B Singapore IPO; Firmus pulling a $5B Sydney float; SoftBank-backed SB Energy delaying a New York listing. (FT)

Investment chiefs were sharply divided on the artificial intelligence build-out at a gathering for alternative investment firms this week, with some pointing to a “once-in-a-lifetime” opportunity and others warning that the data center boom could turn ugly. (BBG)

Banks and investors are becoming increasingly selective and demanding higher returns to fund the massive rollout of artificial intelligence, according to Michael Roberts, head of corporate and institutional banking at HSBC Holdings Plc. (BBG)

Fed's Daly said the Fed will probably need to increase short-term interest rates further to rein in too-high inflation, but she signaled there is no need to do so at the US central bank's October 27-28 meeting. (RTRS)

'Top Forecaster Says Fed May Hike Rates Half a Point in December' Bloomberg article cites Jason Schenker as saying a bigger, half-percentage-point rate increase could be on the table in December. (BBG)

Investors and fund managers predict gold will reach new record highs within two years, supported by strong central bank bullion buying and safe-haven demand amid geopolitical tensions. Provisional World Gold Council data compiled from central bank and IMF figures show central bank gold-buying rose in September to about 63 tonnes, the highest monthly level since November 2024. (FT)

Republicans are playing defense on an expanding electoral map, spending hundreds of millions of dollars in the final stretch of the midterms to prevent a Democratic takeover of Congress as campaigns nationwide reach a fever pitch. (WSJ)

The Trump administration is investigating Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar to build a case to strip her of U.S. citizenship and deport her, according to WSJ citing officials. (WSJ)

The Bank of Japan should not become overly cautious about raising interest rates, given considerable upside risks to inflation, Junko Koeda, a member of its board, said on Thursday, signalling the chance of a near-term hike in borrowing costs. (RTRS)

Japan’s biggest bank is tentatively getting back into the country’s benchmark government bonds, even as it remains concerned that yields could further spike due to fiscal and monetary policies in the nation. (BBG)

Some of Japan's largest asset managers are expected to unveil plans to buy more domestic bonds with markets focusing on whether they would step up divestments of overseas assets to bring money back home. (RTRS)

Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama warned speculators that she was prepared to take action in the currency market again if needed, after the yen touched its weakest level against the dollar this month following hotter US inflation figures. (BBG)

Bloomberg reports investor speculation that China is holding US securities through overseas custodians, potentially explaining Canada’s roughly $600bn Treasury/agency-bond holdings. (BBG)

China must deliver bigger fiscal stimulus as its economy teeters on deflation, a senior International Monetary Fund official said on Thursday. (RTRS)

South Korea’s bank lending to households expanded in September at the slowest pace in six months as softer mortgage growth and a sharp decline in other types of household loans tempered borrowing ahead of a central bank policy decision next week. (BBG)

Singapore new home sales rose in September from a more than two-year low, as developers resumed releasing projects after a brief pause. (BBG)

Australian employment unexpectedly fell in September, with the jobless rate staying at a five-year high of 4.7%, data showed on Thursday, a soft result that quashed the risk of another hike in interest rates this year. (RTRS)

Australians are pulling back at the pump as fuel prices surge, with sales of diesel dropping in August by the most since 2022 and the decline in petrol sales deepening. (BBG)

New Zealand’s interest rate decision in late October is “wide open,” according to Reserve Bank chief economist Paul Conway, even as inflation pressures build. (BBG)

The U.K. economy expanded again in August, helped by a pickup in industrial production, continuing this year’s stronger-than-expected performance despite fears higher energy prices would hinder activity. (WSJ)

A future interest rate increase by the Bank of England should not be interpreted by investors as the start of a long series of increases, BoE Chief Economist Huw Pill said on Thursday. (RTRS)

UK Chancellor John Healey said he will “stay the path” on plans to bring down borrowing over the next few years as he welcomed the International Monetary Fund’s support for the government’s fiscal plans ahead of the budget. (BBG)

London vaults held nearly 10,000 tonnes of gold worth $1.3T last month, supported by central banks diversifying reserves and shifting bullion away from the US amid political uncertainty. (FT)

British government ministers will publish private pensions proposals next spring to boost retirement savings among the self-employed, Pensions Minister Torsten Bell told the FT. (FT)

The European Commission is expected to tell EU leaders that there’s no silver bullet to combat high energy prices, and EU member states are hobbled by price caps and tax cuts that come with a heavy fiscal cost. (BBG)

ECB's Knot said the European Central Bank might need to embrace a policy stance with a modest tilt toward monetary tightening due to economic and geopolitical disruptions. The ECB's current "measured" policy stance "is the right approach to take," according to Knot. (BBG)

A tightening in financial conditions may limit the need for European Central Bank monetary policy action, according to Governing Council member Primoz Dolenc. (BBG)

French government bond issuance is expected to draw attention on Thursday as France’s fiscal challenges remain a source of concern among bond investors. The French Treasury Agency will auction 10 billion euros to 12 billion euros in nominal bonds and 750 million euros to 1.250 billion euros in inflation-linked bonds. (WSJ)

French stocks are lagging their European peers by the widest margin since 2010, as investors demand steep discounts to reflect the country’s challenged public finances and a looming presidential election. (FT)

Italy plans to raise an additional €10.7 billion ($12.00 billion) from the financial sector to help fund its budget over the 2027-2029 period, a government document showed on Thursday. (RTRS)

A proposal for new ethics rules for Norway’s $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund was published by a government-appointed expert committee, including allowing investments in some nuclear stocks and raising the bar on divesting from companies. (BBG)

IRAN:

US military has drawn up fresh Iran strike options that include using the “mother of all bombs” against energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, CNN reports, citing US officials. The plans could be used before or after the midterms if Trump orders combat to resume. (CNN)

The Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global freight rates, a US official said to Reuters. (RTRS)

Russian diesel is expected to reach the American market before the Nov. 3 midterm election, sources told The Post — as fuel costs hit a record $6.53 per gallon last month. The fuel “should be here in the next two weeks if we get everything done,” one American source told The Post, noting Russia agreed to send “a pretty substantial” amount. (Post)

Lufthansa has increased fuelling before flights to Frankfurt as a precautionary step because fuel supplies tighten at Germany's largest air hub due to reduced capacity at a pipeline, the airline said on Thursday. (RTRS)

GEOPOLITICAL:

The US has proposed that European countries unfreeze some Russian sovereign assets immobilised after Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine and transfer them to a vehicle overseen by Washington in an attempt to revive peace talks. (FT)

Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will restart strikes on Russia’s oil refineries as he expressed anger over a “dangerous” withdrawal of US intelligence and simultaneous weakening of Starlink satellite internet service at a time of intense Russian attacks. (FT)

US intelligence officials warned Ukraine’s embassy that further attacks on Russian energy sites would trigger an immediate halt to intelligence sharing, WaPo reports. Its source said intelligence had not been cut off in full, but the threat remained. (WaPo)

Romania reported that a second commercial vessel caught fire near its territorial waters in the space of 12 hours, amid a rise in suspected drone strikes in the Black Sea. (BBG)

US Treasury Secretary Bessent issued a long list of demands for the World Bank in line with Trump administration interests, including ending the bank's prohibition on financing upstream oil and gas projects, putting resources into deep-sea critical minerals mining and reforming its procurement policies. (RTRS)

The west is in a race with China to develop nuclear fusion energy, according to the chief executive of the UK’s state fusion programme, who added that commercialising the nascent technology would arguably be “one of the most important geopolitical events ever”. (FT)

EQUITIES:

TSMC delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook, sustaining torrid growth in defiance of rising concerns about the sustainability of a global AI buildout. Co. maintained its 2026 capex plan of $60 billion to $64 billion. Said it’s mulling Texas for expansion amid discussions with Musk’s Terafab, also reaffirmed it is seeing very strong demand. (BBG)

TSMC said on the call that it would have to run its own fab if it's any part of the Terafab facility, potentially at odds with Elon Musk's statement, “let there be zero doubt,” only his companies would run the Terafab. (BBG)

Data center company Stack Infrastructure Inc. is seeking an A$8.6 billion ($6 billion) loan, according to a Bloomberg sources, in what would be a major test of investor sentiment toward AI debt in the region at a time of mounting concerns. (BBG)

SK Hynix is seeking approval from Washington to export US chipmaking equipment to China to increase production there as a condition for building a factory in the US, according to Reuters sources. (RTRS)

The smartphone market suffered its worst decline on record in the September quarter, after rising memory costs pushed shipments down 22% with worse to come, according to market researcher IDC. (BBG)

Figma's CFO said on Thursday it was uncertain if the design software firm would return to peak gross margin levels as it ramps up AI spending, but said the investments will help draw users and better compete with sophisticated tools from labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. (RTRS)

A merger between Elon Musk’s Tesla Inc. and SpaceX could be announced ahead of the electric-vehicle maker’s annual general meeting, according to analysts at Barclays. (BBG)

ByteDance Ltd. is close to an agreement to buy MediaTek Inc. data center semiconductors, a deal that would secure vital components for TikTok’s owner while helping the Taiwanese chipmaker compete with Qualcomm Inc. (BBG)

TotalEnergies expects its refining margins to have nearly quadrupled in the third quarter compared to last year, as the Iran war continues to lift energy prices and boost profits for oil majors, the French company said in a trading update on Thursday. (RTRS)

Pernod Ricard SA’s sales fell less than expected last quarter as growth in India helped cushion persistent weakness in the US and China. (BBG)

European carmakers are reviving affordable electric retro models, such as Stellantis-owned Citroën's planned €15,000 electric 2CV in 2028 and Volkswagen's ID.Polo inspired by the Golf, to counter a wave of Chinese brands. (FT)

UBS is preparing contingency plans to move its headquarters from Switzerland if Swiss lawmakers proceed with tougher capital requirements. Options under discussion include buying a U.S. financial institution, merging with a European rival or selling itself to a U.S. firm. (WSJ)

EasyJet is facing union opposition to its £5.7 billion ($7.54 billion) takeover by Apollo, but said it was on track to close the deal before the end of the first quarter of 2027. (RTRS)

Private credit funds are in discussions with English football clubs to offer squad-value financing based on the worth of their playing squads, the FT reported, citing specialist football advisers. Similar loans have already been used by clubs in Spain, Portugal, Italy, France and Belgium, and by English second-tier side Burnley, according to FT sources. (FT)

Ericsson set out plans to streamline its operating structure, seeking to strengthen its customer focus and drive efficiencies while warning that higher component costs will be a headwind to profitability next year. (WSJ)

text:
Africa’s First Superpower They Made You Forget.
Alt Afrikaner.

Five pillars make a superpower. Nuclear weapons. A rocket programme reaching for orbit. Synthetic fuel independence. A defence industry ranked tenth on earth. And medical science that led the world. Pre-1994 South Africa had every single one. One country, at the tip of Africa, built all of that before the Berlin Wall came down. Then they made you forget it ever happened.

Now Africa is “just Africa.” Still trying. Still borrowing. Still begging for the infrastructure that one small nation already had, thirty years ago, before it was forced to tear it apart with its own hands.
Let me say something that will offend a lot of people. That is fine. It also happens to be true. While Afrikaners were enriching uranium at Pelindaba, test-firing rockets from the Overberg coast, turning low-grade coal into petrol at Secunda and performing the world’s first human heart transplant at Groote Schuur, the liberation movements across the rest of Africa were being handed a very different gift. Not industrial strategy. Not energy independence. Not sovereign technology. They were handed communism. Slogans instead of centrifuges. Five-year plans instead of fuel plants. Moscow printed the pamphlets. Beijing supplied the rifles. And when the dust settled, every single African state that followed the Soviet model traced the same arc: nationalisation without technical capacity, institutional collapse, structural dependence on the very foreign powers that had supplied the revolution. Tanzania. Mozambique. Zimbabwe. Ethiopia. The pattern is not a coincidence. It is the product.

Communism offered Africa liberation as a brand and dependency as the operating system. It turned “Africa for Africans” into “Africa for anyone with leverage,” and the continent has been paying that bill ever since. Three decades later, the same nations that were told to reject Western industrial models in the name of African socialism are now borrowing billions from Beijing to build what they could have built for themselves, if the one country that had already done it had not been made to dismantle every last piece of it first.
Think about what the Afrikaners actually accomplished. Under crippling international sanctions, with a population smaller than some European cities, they developed an indigenous uranium enrichment process, the Helikon vortex tube, that the outside world had never seen. They built six nuclear weapons and a seventh was on the production line. Then, before handing power to the ANC, the Afrikaner government destroyed them all, signed the Non-Proliferation Treaty, opened every facility to IAEA inspectors, and told the world exactly what they had done. No other nuclear state in history has done that. Not one. They built the bombs, they dismantled the bombs, and they proved it. That is not the behaviour of reckless ideologues. That is discipline on a level the great powers have never matched.

They built a rocket series, RSA-1 through RSA-4, from a coastal launch facility at Overberg near Bredasdorp. RSA-1 hit 100 kilometres. RSA-2 reached 300. The RSA-3, a three-stage solid-propellant satellite launch vehicle based on Israeli Shavit technology, was designed to put a 330-kilogram reconnaissance satellite called Greensat into low Earth orbit. The RSA-4 could lift 550 kilograms to 1,400 kilometres. These were not drawings. They were built. Tested. Operational. And then, under American supervision, the casting pits were filled with concrete, the X-ray equipment was demolished, the test facility at Rooi Els was turned into a nature reserve. Staff went from 500 to 28 in five years. Africa’s only indigenous orbital launch capability was destroyed.

“Precision beats volume. Dignity holds ground.”

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of October 15, 1789, George Washington stepped into his carriage outside the presidential residence on Broadway in New York City and set out for the eastern states. The first session of the new Congress had just adjourned. He was fifty-seven, still recovering from a serious illness the previous summer, and determined that the untried office he now held should not remain a distant abstraction. With him rode his secretaries, Major William Jackson and Tobias Lear, a small staff, and a baggage wagon. Chief Justice John Jay and Secretaries Hamilton and Knox rode with the party as far as the Connecticut line. Washington had written that he wished to become better acquainted with the principal characters and internal circumstances of the states, and to be accessible to people who might offer useful information. He intended to see for himself.

The roads were rough. The autumn countryside of Connecticut was busy with apple harvests. Washington noted in his diary the evidence of British destruction still visible in Norwalk and Fairfield—the standing chimneys of burned houses. He rode into towns astride his great white charger, usually accompanied by local militia, so that the people might see the President of the United States in the flesh rather than learn of him only by proclamation. He stopped at taverns, inspected workshops, walked the streets, and spoke with farmers about soil and crops. On Sundays he attended services at two different Protestant churches, careful not to appear partial to any one denomination.

The climax came at Boston. It was the first time he had returned since he had forced the British to evacuate the city in March 1776. On the morning of October 24 he reached Cambridge by ten. There Lieutenant Governor Samuel Adams and the Executive Council met him. Militia under General Brooks stood in ranks. Washington wore his old military uniform with its gold epaulettes. Church bells rang. Cannon fired from Roxbury, from Dorchester Heights, and from Castle William. A French squadron in the harbor added a royal salute. Citizens lined the streets in groups by trade, each under its own banner. At the State House an arch spanned the street. On one face it read “To the Man who unites all hearts”; on the other, “To Columbia’s favourite Son.” A panel carried the inscription “Boston relieved March 17th 1776.” Above the center rose a canopy crowned by the American Eagle. Washington recorded that the entrance “was in every degree flattering & honorable.”

He stayed several days, dined at Faneuil Hall, inspected the federal arsenal at Springfield, visited early manufactories, and sat for a portrait at the request of the ladies of the town. There were the usual awkwardnesses of the new federal system—Governor Hancock’s attempt to assert state precedence, a brief dispute over who should escort the President into the city—but the people themselves left no doubt of their feeling. When he moved on, fireworks marked his departure from Massachusetts. In New Hampshire the reception was scarcely less grand. At the Merrimack he was met by hundreds of cavalry. In Portsmouth he inspected the harbor by boat and attended both Episcopal and Presbyterian services. Everywhere he recorded what he saw: the condition of the land, the energy of the people, the state of manufactures, the disposition toward the new government.

He returned to New York on November 13 having visited nearly sixty towns. The Constitution was only months old. Many Americans still thought of themselves first as citizens of their own commonwealths. Washington had chosen not to govern solely from the temporary capital. He had taken the office into the country itself, riding the roads, sleeping in taverns, listening, and letting the people look upon the man who now held the highest civil office in the republic.

text:
Deconstructing Dark Bay
(Behind the Scenes, Part Two: Supporting Characters)

It wasn’t just the pace I tinkered with in Dark Bay; I also leaned heavily on my characters to create the chilling narrative in a slightly unusual manner.

Dark Bay has a single main character and relies on only a handful of supporting figures—a deliberate stylistic choice meant to magnify the MC’s isolation from the world. While the novel also contains numerous minor characters, their impact is limited. However, the five figures below do far more than support the plot: each functions as a living metaphor that both advances the narrative and deepens our understanding of the MC.

Luther (the bathroom dealer)

Luther offers the MC his first clear look at what the underworld demands, and he is the one who places the full weight of a promise on the protagonist. The two eventually become close friends, yet Luther is more than a friend or mentor—he is the MC’s mirror image in reverse. Where the MC is sliding from ordinary life into crime, Luther is moving in the opposite direction. They are the Yin and Yang of the book, a duality reinforced by the fact that the MC is white while Luther is Black. As one steps into the life, the other steps out of it, each occupying the space the other abandons.

Jack (the silver-haired man)

Jack is the gatekeeper who opens the door into organized crime. “Hey kid, got twenty minutes to do me a favor?” is the line that starts everything; those twenty minutes become a lifetime. A powerful Irish-American Gambino associate focused on money laundering, he almost becomes a father figure to the MC, offering a path toward independence. That relationship ends abruptly when Jack introduces the MC to Sammy “The Bull” Gravano.

Sammy “The Bull” Gravano

Sammy is portrayed realistically—neither a Hollywood caricature nor the version of himself he presents on his podcasts. He speaks like a thug, yet he is far more intelligent than he is generally credited with being, and he often runs the family in all but name.

When he “asks” the MC to play an auxiliary role in Paul Castellano’s assassination, the request is not really a request. The MC understands that his invisibility is beginning to fade. Later, Sammy’s line “You’re with me now” sharpens the point. The wording is deliberate: it is “me,” not “us.” The distinction is small, but the MC registers it at once.

Through Sammy, organized crime stops being an abstract force and becomes personal. The MC receives a brutal awakening—he can no longer stay invisible.

Michael DeBatt (Big Mike / Mike Colombo)

Michael is depicted exactly as I knew him during that period. He arrives at the bay claiming to be someone he is not and is already both an alcoholic and a heavy cocaine user. The MC quickly realizes Mike is not entirely truthful, yet forms a bond with the unraveling man. Both are educated mafia associates who see through the self-perpetuated myths of the Mob. Mike is also the only one who clearly recognizes the MC’s dissociation from society, likening him to a robot.

The tragedy arrives later: Mike is grudgingly marked for death by Sammy, and the MC is given the contract. He knows refusal is suicidal and will not save Mike—someone else will simply take the job. He accepts while planning to save his friend. Mike is a glimpse of the MC’s most probable fate.

Jane

Jane is perhaps the least and most understood character. On the surface she is the woman the MC loves, even though he never tells her. Her presence, however, is a metaphor for something larger. Despite his calculated detachment, his repressed passion culminates in one of the novel’s most emotionally raw lines:

“I kissed her as if she was life itself and the universe would end the second I stopped.”

The moment underscores the crushing irony of his existence. He is capable of intense, consuming love, yet the criminal path he accepted has already sealed his fate, ensuring he cannot hold onto “life itself.”

These supporting characters do more than populate the world around the MC—they define the boundaries of the isolation he has chosen, the metaphors he embodies, and the costs he will ultimately pay.

The principal transmission mechanism is a longer period of equipment purchases, installation, qualification, and subsequent service demand. New N2 capacity and additional N3 fabs require manufacturing tools before commercial wafer production begins. Equipment suppliers can therefore recognize economic benefits ahead of the foundry revenue supported by those investments.

Process complexity adds another dimension. Nanosheet transistors, tighter manufacturing tolerances, and increasingly sophisticated interconnects support demand for deposition, etch, inspection, and metrology. Applied Materials and Lam have relevant materials-engineering exposure; KLA benefits from the need to identify defects and control increasingly difficult processes; Tokyo Electron participates across multiple manufacturing steps. These are category-level transmission mechanisms, not evidence of specific market-share gains.

Tool inflation supports pricing resilience but does not prove that every supplier’s gross margin will expand. Suppliers face their own input costs, product development requirements, and customer negotiations. In addition, some capacity growth will come from tool conversions and productivity improvements rather than entirely new equipment.

Near-term catalyst: Greater confidence in order duration and fab readiness, not an automatic 2026 earnings upgrade. Longer-duration shift: A broader, geographically distributed investment cycle through 2027 and 2028 supports a more durable equipment opportunity. The strongest conclusion is sustained demand visibility, not a precise percentage increase in any supplier’s revenue.

ASML BENEFITS FROM EXPANSION, WHILE HIGH-NA MIX EXPECTATIONS REQUIRE TIMING DISCIPLINE (READ-THROUGH 7)

Affected company: ASML Holding (ASML: Netherlands). Direction: Positive for overall lithography demand; negative only relative to expectations requiring rapid TSMC High-NA adoption before 2030. Magnitude: High longer-term importance, but limited incremental near-term surprise.

TSMC’s N2 expansion and additional N3 fabs support demand for conventional EUV capacity and related services. At the same time, Wei reiterated planned High-NA adoption around 2030, emphasizing that new equipment must offer suitable technology, reasonable cost, and sufficient maturity. The call also referenced collaboration on 12-inch photomasks by 2031.

The key distinction is between aggregate lithography spending and the timing of migration to a more expensive platform. ASML can benefit materially from TSMC’s expansion even if TSMC continues using conventional EUV longer than some competitors. Delayed High-NA adoption is not equivalent to lost lithography spending, particularly when leading-edge production capacity is increasing.

Conversely, forecasts that assume a rapid TSMC-driven High-NA revenue mix shift during 2027 or 2028 are not supported by this commentary. The larger-mask program is also a separate development timeline. The associated 2031 target concerns a pilot capability, rather than immediate broad commercial production.

Near-term catalyst: The capacity expansion is constructive, while High-NA timing is primarily a confirmation of an already disclosed roadmap rather than a new delay. Longer-duration shift: ASML retains a critical role in both the current expansion and the eventual High-NA transition. The investment implication is to distinguish durable customer spending from optimistic assumptions about product mix and adoption dates.

MEMORY

HBM DEMAND RECEIVES A STRONGER CROSS-CHECK, NOT A GUARANTEE OF PRICING OR SHARE (READ-THROUGH 8)

Affected companies: SK hynix (000660: South Korea); Micron Technology (MU: United States). Direction: Positive. Magnitude: High relevance to their AI memory businesses and potentially material to consolidated earnings.

The supporting call evidence is sustained accelerator demand, HPC growth, and the expansion of advanced packaging capacity. TSMC described production at 5x reticle scale and development toward larger assemblies. The read-through is strongest when combined with established product relationships: both SK hynix and Micron have disclosed HBM4 involvement in NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin ecosystem.

The transmission mechanism is the conversion of greater accelerator output into demand for qualified high-bandwidth memory. Logic manufacturing and advanced packaging capacity are complementary to memory shipments. Successful expansion across these bottlenecks increases the amount of complete accelerator hardware that can be delivered, supporting HBM utilization and revenue opportunities.

Larger package formats provide room for more sophisticated compute and memory integration, but package size alone does not establish HBM content per device. The positive conclusion rests primarily on greater accelerator demand and manufacturing capacity, not an assumed linear relationship between reticle multiples and memory revenue.

Near-term catalyst: Stronger confidence in AI memory demand ahead of supplier results and customer platform ramps. Longer-duration shift: A larger installed accelerator base and more complex systems support a durable market for qualified HBM suppliers. The call does not establish future HBM prices, supplier allocation shares, or a uniform benefit across commodity DRAM and NAND. Nor does it prove that memory supply is currently sufficient to satisfy every planned accelerator shipment.

ELECTRONIC DESIGN AUTOMATION

MORE CUSTOMER DESIGNS AND LARGER PACKAGES SUPPORT EDA SPENDING BEFORE FAB OUTPUT ARRIVES (READ-THROUGH 9)

Affected companies: Synopsys (SNPS: United States); Cadence Design Systems (CDNS: United States). Direction: Positive. Magnitude: Moderate consolidated financial relevance, with high strategic importance to advanced-node and system-design demand.

TSMC reported greater customer activity around A14 than at the comparable stage of N2 and maintained the 2028 volume-production schedule. It also described increasingly large advanced packages and simultaneous smartphone and HPC participation in new-node ramps. These comments point to a substantial design workload before the associated manufacturing revenue materializes.

The transmission mechanism is additional demand for implementation, verification, signoff, interface IP, and multiphysics analysis. Smaller geometries and larger multi-die systems create interacting timing, power, thermal, signal-integrity, and manufacturability problems. Synopsys and Cadence have established TSMC ecosystem relationships covering advanced processes and packaging, making this a direct technical exposure rather than a generic software read-through.

The timing differs from equipment and wafer production. Customers need design tools and validated flows while developing products, often well before volume manufacturing. A14 engagement can therefore support EDA activity during 2026 and 2027 even though meaningful wafer production is scheduled for 2028.

Near-term catalyst: Increased confidence in advanced-design activity and customer spending priorities. Longer-duration shift: Greater system complexity supports the value of comprehensive design and verification platforms. The call does not establish specific bookings, license-price increases, or immediate revenue acceleration, and EDA revenue does not scale mechanically with TSMC wafer capacity.

DATA-CENTER ELECTRICAL AND THERMAL INFRASTRUCTURE

PHYSICAL PROJECT VALIDATION SUPPORTS POWER AND COOLING DEMAND, NOT A GENERAL POWER-SCARCITY TRADE (READ-THROUGH 10)

Affected companies: Vertiv Holdings (VRT: United States); Eaton (ETN: Ireland); Schneider Electric (SU: France). Direction: Positive. Magnitude: High relevance to AI-facing infrastructure businesses; moderate consolidated read-through for the more diversified suppliers.

TSMC disclosed that it is sending teams to inspect US data-center construction and power availability. Management described the feedback as “so far so good” and said cloud service providers had prepared well. This is a meaningful physical-project cross-check because it comes from a manufacturer making large capital commitments against future customer demand.

The mechanism is greater confidence that semiconductor demand is associated with infrastructure capable of progressing toward deployment. Completed data centers require power distribution, conversion, protection, and cooling. Vertiv has direct exposure to thermal management and critical power; Eaton and Schneider participate through electrical distribution and related infrastructure.

The less obvious implication is that adequate power preparation is positive for equipment demand even if it reduces fears of grid shortages. Infrastructure suppliers benefit when projects are built and commissioned. They do not require an acute electricity shortage to generate revenue. Vertiv’s disclosed work on NVIDIA-aligned power and cooling infrastructure provides a concrete example of the connection between advanced computing platforms and facility-level equipment.

Near-term catalyst: Reduced concern that power constraints will derail a large share of announced AI projects. Longer-duration shift: Continued physical deployment supports equipment demand through subsequent construction and commissioning phases. The call does not identify which sites were inspected, which vendors supply them, or whether orders are incremental to existing backlogs. It also does not establish higher merchant electricity prices or provide a sufficient basis for a blanket bullish call on power generators.

CLOUD PLATFORMS AND INTERNET

STRONGER DEPLOYMENT VISIBILITY DOES NOT REMOVE THE CASH-FLOW BURDEN OF AI (READ-THROUGH 11)

Affected companies: Microsoft (MSFT: United States); https://t.co/SpqvHNUxpK (AMZN: United States); Alphabet (GOOGL: United States); Meta Platforms (META: United States). Direction: Positive for infrastructure availability, negative for near-term cash-flow conversion and eventual depreciation burden. Magnitude: High financial relevance, but the net equity impact depends on monetization.

The call combines strong cloud service provider demand signals with expensive capacity expansion and acknowledged tool, material, and labor inflation. Management described strategic pricing differentiated by technology and manufacturing location, including US production. It did not quantify broad customer price increases or disclose revised hyperscaler budgets.

The negative transmission mechanism is the financial requirement to acquire and operate more sophisticated infrastructure. Capital expenditure reduces cash flow before the associated assets necessarily generate adequate revenue or productivity benefits. Once equipment is placed into service, depreciation affects earnings over its useful life. Geographic diversification and more complex systems can add cost even when headline computational efficiency improves.

The positive mechanism is greater deployment capacity. Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet can use additional infrastructure to expand cloud and AI services, while Meta’s economic benefits are more closely linked to its own applications and advertising systems. More available compute can relieve service constraints, but TSMC’s manufacturing demand does not prove the ultimate return on that investment.

Near-term catalyst: The call reduces concern about physical deployment feasibility while reinforcing scrutiny of upcoming capital expenditure and free-cash-flow guidance. Longer-duration shift: A larger infrastructure base creates both revenue potential and a more substantial fixed-cost burden. TSMC did not identify the customers whose sites it inspected, so the assessment is sector-level rather than confirmation of a particular company’s projects.

The cross-portfolio asymmetry is important: a stronger semiconductor order outlook can be immediately favorable for suppliers while remaining financially mixed for the buyers. Long positions in semiconductor suppliers and hyperscalers are therefore not interchangeable expressions of the same earnings catalyst.

SMARTPHONE AND CONSUMER SEMICONDUCTORS

LEADING-EDGE STRENGTH SHOULD NOT BE MISTAKEN FOR A BROAD HANDSET RECOVERY (READ-THROUGH 12)

Affected companies: MediaTek (2454: Taiwan); Qualcomm (QCOM: United States). Direction: Negative for expectations of a broad, volume-led handset recovery; mixed for consolidated performance because premium products can remain strong. Magnitude: Moderate, with greater relevance to price-sensitive handset exposure.

Management stated that consumer and price-sensitive end markets were being challenged by “rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties.” This warning accompanied strong leading-edge demand and a 10% sequential increase in TSMC smartphone revenue. The combination supports a bifurcated market rather than a uniform recovery.

The transmission mechanism is pressure on handset affordability and manufacturer economics. Higher component costs can lead to higher retail prices, lower manufacturer margins, specification reductions, or more conservative production plans. Qualcomm and MediaTek can consequently experience weaker unit demand or unfavorable customer mix even while premium application processors migrate to more advanced manufacturing technologies.

TSMC’s smartphone revenue growth does not resolve that tension because it combines volume, product mix, process value, and seasonal manufacturing patterns. Revenue can increase as more expensive chips enter production without establishing a comparable recovery in end-market handset units. MediaTek’s advanced-node development and Qualcomm’s flagship platforms provide offsets, but neither eliminates the cost sensitivity of the broader customer base.

Near-term catalyst: Increased downside sensitivity around handset shipment guidance, inventory commentary, and component-cost pass-through. Longer-duration shift: Greater differentiation between premium platforms and price-sensitive devices, rather than a broad semiconductor consumer upcycle. The call supports caution toward extrapolating AI-led foundry strength into handset unit assumptions; it does not establish an immediate company-specific earnings miss.

Across these segments, the highest-conviction portfolio conclusion is that AI spending is broadening while remaining concentrated in a shared economic driver. CPU, accelerator, networking, memory, equipment, and power-infrastructure suppliers monetize different stages of the same deployment cycle. Owning companies across those stages reduces individual product risk, but it does not eliminate exposure to a synchronized change in cloud capital spending, project completion, or infrastructure returns.

Today in History 
October 15th
1860
An 11-Year-Old Girl Conv inces Abraham Lincoln to Grow a Beard

On October 15, 1860, an 11-year-old girl named Grace Bedell from Westfield, New York, wrote a letter that would help change the appearance of one of America’s most recognizable presidents. Her recipient was Abraham Lincoln, the Republican candidate for president, who was campaigning against Stephen Douglas, John C. Breckinridge, and John Bell in one of the most consequential elections in American history.

At the time, Lincoln was clean-shaven, with a long, angular face and prominent cheekbones. Grace had seen his portrait on a campaign picture and believed that growing a beard would improve his appearance and help him win votes.

In her letter, Grace explained that she had four brothers, some of whom supported Lincoln. She promised that if he grew whiskers, she would try to persuade the others to vote for him, although she was too young to vote herself. She offered an amusing observation: women liked whiskers, and they might persuade their husbands to support Lincoln if he grew a beard.

Grace wrote, “You would look a great deal better for your face is so thin.” She also asked Lincoln to write back, signing her letter affectionately.

Surprisingly, Lincoln responded on October 19, 1860, just four days later. Writing from Springfield, Illinois, he thanked Grace for her suggestion but wondered whether growing whiskers might seem like an artificial attempt to improve his appearance. He asked whether people would consider it an affectation, since he had never worn a beard before.

Nevertheless, Lincoln soon began growing facial hair. When he won the presidential election on November 6, 1860, his beard was beginning to develop. Over the following months, it became the distinctive full beard that Americans would associate with him throughout the Civil War.

The most memorable chapter of their story occurred on February 16, 1861. Lincoln was traveling by train from Illinois to Washington, D.C., for his inauguration. When his train stopped in Westfield, New York, he addressed the gathered crowd and mentioned the young girl who had written to him months earlier.

Lincoln explained that he had acted partly upon her suggestion and asked whether Grace was present. When she was brought forward, Lincoln stepped down to greet her and kissed her on the cheek. By then, he was wearing a full beard. The touching encounter delighted spectators and was reported in newspapers across the country.

Lincoln would become the first American president to wear a full beard, and his appearance would become inseparable from his historical image. Although historians cannot establish that Grace’s letter was the sole reason for his decision, Lincoln himself publicly acknowledged her influence.

The story carries particular significance because it unfolded during a period of mounting national crisis. Southern states were beginning to secede following Lincoln’s election, and the country stood on the brink of civil war. Amid these extraordinary tensions, the future president still found time to acknowledge the thoughtful suggestion of a child.

Grace Bedell’s letter remains one of the most charming pieces of presidential correspondence in American history. Preserved for future generations, it demonstrates how an ordinary young citizen, without political power or influence, could leave a lasting mark on the public image of a president. #OTD

text:
A 1,000-pound animal that makes wolves think twice stood ten feet from a stranger holding wire cutters.
She did not charge.
She did not run.
She did not even flinch.
She waited.
Sixty seconds. Watch the mother. Not the man. The mother.
I have seen this clip more times than I will admit in public, and I still cannot decide which moment wrecked me the hardest. I have a favorite now. It happens at the very end. If you scroll away before it, you will never know why I am writing 4,000 words about a minute of video.
Here is the thing nobody tells you about a moment like this: the most dangerous creature in the frame is also the most patient one.
Let me explain why that should be impossible.
1/ FIRST, UNDERSTAND WHAT SHE IS
A cow moose is not a deer. Stop picturing a deer.
Picture a living wall that weighs as much as a grand piano, stands taller at the shoulder than most men stand at the top of their head, and carries legs like steel posts with hooves the size of dinner plates. A full-grown cow runs somewhere around 800 to 1,000 pounds. A bull can push 1,500. They are the largest members of the deer family on Earth, and they are built like something that was supposed to go extinct with the mammoths and somehow forgot.
They can run about 35 miles per hour through brush. They can stomp a wolf into the snow. They can kick forward, backward, and sideways with a speed that makes people at the ER stop asking questions. In parts of North America, wildlife managers will quietly tell you that moose put more people in hospitals than bears do. Not because moose hunt anyone. Because moose do not negotiate.
And the single most dangerous version of a moose is not the giant bull with the antlers on the postcard.
It is a mother with a calf.
2/ THE ONE RULE EVERY LOCAL KNOWS
Ask anyone who lives where moose live. Ask the guy at the gas station. Ask the woman who has plowed the same road for thirty winters. They will give you the same rule in the same flat voice:
Never get between a cow and her calf.
Not a suggestion. A law of physics. Every year, people who know better walk a little too close for a photo and learn the rule the hard way. Her ears pin back. The hair along her neck stands up. She licks her lips. Then she is on you, and there is no version of the next three seconds where you are the one in charge.
A mother moose does not weigh risk. She does not calculate odds. Her entire nervous system has been reduced, by a few million years of evolution, to one instruction written in capital letters: THE BABY LIVES.
Now hold that thought. Hold it tight.
Because what you are about to see is a mother whose baby is in the worst trouble of its short life, and every instinct in her body should be screaming at her to destroy anything that moves.
And she does the opposite.
3/ THE COLDEST HOUR OF THE DAY
There is a specific kind of morning in the high country, usually in autumn, when the sun has not quite decided to show up yet. The sky goes the color of a peach left in a freezer. The grass turns white and crunches. Your breath hangs in front of your face like a ghost that does not want to leave.
Temperatures drop below freezing. Everything is quiet. Everything is stiff. Every living thing out there is running on a short supply of heat.
For a newborn animal, that hour is not scenery. It is a countdown.
A young calf has a fraction of an adult's body mass, a thin coat, and almost no fat reserve. A freezing morning can turn a small problem into a fatal one with brutal speed. Add a second problem on top of the first, and you have the exact situation where wilderness stops being a postcard and starts being a math equation nobody wants to solve.
Hold that image. The frost. The cold. The mother. The clock.
Now add one more ingredient. Add the thing that has been quietly killing wildlife across the American West for a hundred and fifty years.
4/ THE INVENTION THAT CLOSED A CONTINENT
In 1874, an Illinois farmer named Joseph Glidden patented a twisted strand of wire with sharp barbs spaced along it. It was cheap. It was light. It could be strung across a thousand miles of prairie without a single tree to nail it to.
It changed everything.
Open range, the thing that defined the American West, was gone within a generation. Cattle ranchers wired in their land. Farmers wired in their crops. Entire cultures of nomads, bison, pronghorn, and elk found themselves facing a new kind of wall that did not look like a wall. It looked like nothing. Four thin lines of metal you could barely see at dusk.
Western wildlife agencies still spend years and serious money retrofitting fences for one reason: animals do not understand wire. They understand ground. They understand air. They understand leaping. And young ones, especially, have not yet learned that something nearly invisible can hold them like a trap.
A calf's leg slides between two strands. The animal panics. It pulls. The barbs bite. It pulls harder. Every instinct says run, and every attempt to run tightens the problem.
Biologists have a grim phrase for what happens next. They do not use it lightly, and I will not repeat it here.
This is the story behind the story. This is why the minute you are about to watch is not cute. It is a rescue against an invisible enemy.
5/ POWER WITHOUT HANDS
Here is the tragedy hiding inside the frame.
Think about what a moose is. Absolute strength. Absolute size. Absolute will. She could win a fight against almost anything on four legs in the Rocky Mountains.
And she cannot undo a single piece of twisted wire.
She has no fingers. No thumbs. No pliers. No plan. All the power in the world, and not one ounce of it is useful for the job in front of her. She can only stand there, a few feet away, close enough to feel the calf's heartbeat in the air, and watch the clock.
I think that image has haunted me more than any special effects shot I have ever seen. A creature that is the strongest thing for ten miles, completely helpless, because the problem requires the one thing she does not have.
Hands.
There is exactly one species in that valley that has them.
And that species is the thing she has been told, by every generation of her ancestors, to run from.
6/ THE MOST EXPENSIVE DECISION IN THE ANIMAL KINGDOM
Let me tell you about trust, because that is the real subject here.
For wild animals, trust is not a feeling. It is a financial instrument, and the interest rate is death.
Every wild animal runs a constant background calculation. Is that shape a threat? Is that sound a predator? Is that smell a mistake I only make once? Get it wrong in one direction, and you die. Get it wrong in the other direction, and you waste calories running from a harmless branch, which, over a long winter, also kills you.
Humans have been on the wrong side of that equation for ten thousand years. We hunt. We build roads. We fence. We shoot. We are, by any honest measurement, the apex predator of every ecosystem we touch.
So the baseline setting for a moose looking at a person is simple. Danger. Leave. Now.
For that setting to flip, something extraordinary has to happen. Researchers who study wild animal behavior have documented that many species are remarkably good at telling humans apart. Crows remember individual faces for years. Deer in parks learn which people carry food and which carry cameras. Some animals appear to read body language: pace, posture, where a person's eyes go, whether they approach head-on or at an angle, whether they are loud or quiet.
A slow walker. Shoulders down. Voice low. No sudden movement. Giving the animal room to decide.
Is that enough? Can an animal truly tell the difference between a threat and a helper?
I do not know. Nobody fully does. Science is honest about the limits here, and so am I.
But I know what I watched.
7/ THE SIXTY-SECOND RULE I NOW BELIEVE IN
Most viral videos die in the first three seconds. The editing is frantic. The music is aggressive. The caption screams at you.
This one does the reverse. It does almost nothing. It waits. It is quiet. It lets you sit inside the tension for so long that you begin to feel it in your own shoulders.
That is not an accident of the medium. That is the whole trick, the oldest trick in storytelling, older than film, older than books, older than writing itself:
Make the audience afraid of something that has not happened yet.
You know what you are afraid of, even if you cannot say it out loud. You are afraid of the moment the mother decides she has seen enough. You are afraid of the second calf. You are afraid of the wire. You are afraid of the cold. You are afraid of the person, because a person is fragile and a moose is not.
And through all of that, one single thing keeps happening that you did not expect, and I will not tell you what it is.
I will only say that around the halfway point, my own breathing changed.
And here is the cruel part about attention: you will want to look at the man, because the man is the one doing something. The man is the plot. But the plot is not the point. The point is standing a few feet away, absolutely motionless, and she is doing the hardest thing in the entire video.
8/ THE COMMITTEE
Every rescue has a supervisory committee. I did not know that until now.
There is always someone standing in the background with strong opinions and zero responsibility. Someone who arrived late and stayed long. Someone who is, technically, helping, in the sense that they are present, and presence is a kind of moral support if you squint.
In this case, the committee was larger than I have ever seen on a job like this. It had members who did not speak any language the rescuer knows. It had members who do not use language at all. It had members who looked, frankly, deeply skeptical of his methods.
Nobody offered feedback on his technique. Nobody asked about his credentials. Nobody posted a one-star review.
They simply watched, with the calm, serious attention of people who have seen too many things go wrong and have decided, this once, to hope.
If you have ever tried to do a delicate job with an audience, you know exactly how heavy that feels. Now imagine the audience is not your neighbors.
Imagine the audience weighs half a ton.
9/ THE PART THAT BROKE THE PLOT
Right about the time you think you understand what kind of video this is, it changes.
I will not spoil how. I will say this: the title of the clip is a joke about the supervisors, and for about thirty seconds I treated the whole thing as a joke too. Cute animals, funny framing, nice morning.
Then the story did something I did not see coming, and it stopped being about one animal, one fence, one problem. It became about a pattern.
A pattern of what happens when a stranger does not look away.
A pattern of what happens when someone with the tools, the hands, and the time decides that the problem in front of them is theirs.
There is no big speech. There is no swelling soundtrack. There is no slow-motion hero shot. There is a quiet person, a cold morning, and a job that has to be done carefully because the margin for error is the size of a leg.
I have watched grown men on the internet cry at a Super Bowl ad. This clip did something stranger. It made me feel calm and furious in the same breath, calm at what the person did, and furious that the world is built in such a way that this person had to.
10/ WHY YOUR BRAIN CANNOT LOOK AWAY
There is a name for the feeling you get from watching a stranger do something unexpectedly good. The psychologist Jonathan Haidt calls it elevation. It is a warm, chest-level sensation, and research on it points to something fascinating: people who feel elevated are more likely to help someone in the next few hours. Kindness, it turns out, is contagious, and the delivery system is a story.
That is why this kind of video travels. Not because it is sweet. Because it is functional. A rescue clip is, in effect, a small dose of a behavior your species wants to repeat.
There is also an older, more primitive layer under it. Your brain is a prediction machine, and tension is a prediction waiting to be resolved. Fear sets the prediction. Time stretches it. When the story finally pays off, your brain releases the pressure, and the pleasure of that release is real, chemical, and slightly addictive.
Great storytellers have always known this. The good ones do not rush the release. They make you wait.
This video makes you wait.
It makes you wait with a mother, a stranger, and a wire, and by the time the release comes, you have forgotten you are holding your breath.
11/ WHAT THE MOTHER KNEW
I keep coming back to her.
Because the stranger is easy to understand. Humans help. We are weirdly good at it, for a species with such a violent history. There is a reason every culture on Earth has a story about the person who stopped on the road.
The mother is the mystery.
What does a mother moose know that lets her stay still? Not run. Not strike. Stand. Let a creature she has every reason to distrust reach toward her most precious thing.
I have tried a dozen theories. Maybe she is exhausted. Maybe she is calculating. Maybe she is a particular moose with a particular history. Maybe she has seen this person before, and knows exactly who he is, and what his hands have done.
Maybe it is simply that in the moment of true need, fear and hope trade places, and she chose hope.
I do not know. I will never know. And that uncertainty is the exact reason this clip sticks in your head like a splinter. Because it suggests a version of the world where the gap between predator and protector is narrower than we assume, and can be crossed in a single morning, in the cold, with nothing but patience.
12/ THE NUMBERS NOBODY PUTS IN THE CAPTION
A few facts, because I think they matter.
Moose calves weigh around 30 pounds at birth. By the time they are a few months old, they can pack on a pound or two a day, a growth rate that looks absurd on paper. Twins are common when the food is good. Calves usually stay with their mother for about a year, until she drives them off before the next spring brings new babies.
That first autumn and winter are the most dangerous stretch of any moose's life. Predators. Disease. Parasites. Deep snow. Bad luck. A young moose that makes it through its first year has beaten odds that would make a casino blush.
Now stack a barbed wire fence on top of those odds.
The fence is not a natural threat. It is a human-made one, which means it is the one problem in this story that a human is uniquely able to fix.
Wildlife agencies in several Western states publish simple guidelines for building fences that animals can survive. The commonly recommended version: keep the top strand no higher than about 40 inches so adults can clear it, make the bottom strand smooth and at least 16 inches off the ground so fawns and calves can slip under without catching a leg, and mark the wire so it stops being invisible.
That is it. Forty inches. Sixteen inches. A change you could make in a single weekend.
The difference between a minute like the one you are about to watch and a very different ending can come down to a few inches of wire.
13/ THE MATH OF ONE MORNING
Let me do the arithmetic, because the arithmetic is what makes my hands go cold.
One frozen field. One invisible line of metal. One small animal with a leg in the wrong place. One mother with no tools. One clock running down at the speed of the temperature.
Now count the things that had to go right.
Someone had to be awake at that hour. Someone had to notice. Someone had to walk over instead of drive past. Someone had to own the right pair of cutters, and keep them within reach, and know how to use them without turning a bad situation into a worse one. Someone had to move slowly enough that a 1,000-pound mother decided not to make it personal.
That is five coincidences stacked in a row. Remove any single one and the clip does not exist. The morning just ends differently, quietly, out of frame, and nobody ever writes a word about it.
This is the thing I cannot shake. For every minute of video like this that reaches your phone, how many identical mornings happen with no one there?
14/ THE UNEXPECTED SECOND CHARACTER
I will give you one more teaser, and then I am done.
There is a second animal in the clip.
Not a moose. Not a bystander. A character with its own arc.
At first, you will think it has nothing to do with the story. Then you will realize that it has everything to do with the story. By the end, you will find yourself rooting for it with an intensity that surprised me, because I did not even know I had picked a side.
That second character delivers the scene I keep replaying.
I will tell you only this: it involves a fence, a person, and a decision that animals are not supposed to be capable of making.
Do not skip ahead. Seriously. The setup matters. If you jump to the end, you will see a nice moment. If you sit through the whole thing, you will see why it is not nice. It is earned.
15/ THE LAST FIFTEEN SECONDS
Every great clip has a final beat, and this one has the best I have seen in a long time.
It is quiet. It is small. It takes less than fifteen seconds.
And it answers a question you did not realize you were asking.
When it ended, I did what I always do: I looked for the catch. The twist. The cynical edit. The little tell that says this was staged for likes.
I did not find one.
What I found instead was something I had forgotten I wanted to see. A family, together, moving off into a cold bright morning like nothing had happened. As if the whole thing had been small. As if it had been routine.
It was not routine.
It was the single best sixty seconds I have watched this year, and I did not know it was coming.
16/ THE HONEST VERSION OF HEROISM
We have a bad definition of heroism.
We think it looks like a cape. A siren. A camera. A speech.
Real heroism usually looks like a person in a tired old jacket crouching in the frost, working carefully with cold hands on a job that nobody asked them to do, with no guarantee it will work, and no one clapping.
There is no brand deal in that image. No hashtag. No follow-for-follow.
There is just a person who saw a problem and decided it was their problem.
I think that is the quiet reason this clip is spreading. Not the animals, though the animals are magnificent. Not the setting, though the light is almost unfair. It is the simple, almost forgotten idea that competence plus kindness is a superpower, and ordinary people can have it on any random Tuesday.
Most of the content we scroll past is designed to make us feel small, angry, or behind. This is the opposite. It is a minute that makes you feel like the world might be a little better than the feed insists.
That is a rare product. Protect it. Share it.
17/ WHAT I THINK THE ANIMALS UNDERSTOOD
Here is the thought that will not leave me alone.
We spend enormous energy arguing about whether animals think, feel, grieve, or hope. Scientists write papers. Philosophers write essays. People shout in comment sections.
And then a clip like this appears, and the whole argument quietly dissolves.
Because you do not need a paper to read what a mother's body is saying when she holds still. You do not need a study to understand why a herd stays close, why a small animal presses against a person's leg, or why a group of enormous creatures can wait in silence for a rescue to finish.
You already know what that is.
You have known since you were a child.
It is trust. It is also fear. It is also a kind of hope that is strong enough to beat the fear.
And I am not sure humans have a monopoly on any of it.
18/ THE QUESTION I KEEP ASKING MYSELF
If it were me, what would I do?
Would I walk toward a frozen field full of animals that could end me in two seconds? Would I keep my voice steady? Would I trust my hands? Would I stay calm while something huge and unpredictable watched every move?
Honestly, I do not know.
I like to believe I would help. Most people do. But believing and doing are separated by a gap, and the gap is filled with fear, and fear is a very persuasive roommate.
That is why I watch this clip the way some people watch a master craftsman at work. Not to be entertained. To study. To see what steady looks like, up close, in real conditions, with real stakes.
And to ask myself, again and again, the smaller version of the same question:
What small, difficult, slightly frightening thing is in front of me right now that I keep telling myself is someone else's job?
19/ WHY I AM WRITING THIS AT ALL
I could have just posted the video with a heart emoji.
That is the standard move. Clip, caption, done. Move on to the next one.
But some videos deserve a longer conversation. Not because they need explaining. Because they are doorways. They open something in a person that a quick scroll never reaches.
And I think we are all starving for that right now. For something that is not outrage. For something that is not an ad. For something that makes you say, out loud, to nobody, in your kitchen at midnight: wow.
If you made it this far, you are already the kind of person who is going to love this.
So here is my ask.
Go watch it. All of it. Do not skip. Do not speed it up. Do not do the thing where you check the progress bar to see how much is left.
Let it be slow. Let it be cold. Let the mother stand there.
Let yourself not know what happens next.
20/ WHEN YOU FINISH
When it ends, do three things for me.
First, notice how you feel. Not what you think. What you feel. Where it lands in your body. That feeling is data. It is telling you something about what you want more of in your life.
Second, tell one person. Not a group chat. One person. Send it with no context, just the link and the words: watch the mother. See what they say back.
Third, if you live anywhere near a fence line, a ranch, a pasture, a trail, or a road that crosses wildlife country, remember the numbers. Forty inches at the top. Sixteen at the bottom. Smooth wire low. Marked wire high. Small changes, enormous consequences.
The whole story we just talked about lives in those few inches.
21/ THE REPLIES I ALREADY KNOW I AM GOING TO GET
Someone will say it is staged. It is not obvious to me that it is, but I understand the reflex, and I respect the skepticism. Watch it for the little things that are hard to fake. The cold. The breath. The way no one in the frame looks at a camera.
Someone will say the moose should be left alone, that nature should take its course. That is a serious position, held by serious people, and the answer is complicated. But a fence is not nature. A fence is us. When our own structure traps a wild animal, the question of whether to intervene is not the same as meddling in a predator and prey chase.
Someone will say they were scared the entire time. Good. So was I.
Someone will say they cried. Me too. Zero shame.
Someone will say the supervisors deserve credit. They do.
And someone, I promise, will ask for a part two.
22/ THE SHORTEST VERSION OF THIS ENTIRE POST
If you scrolled straight to the bottom, here is the whole thing in one paragraph.
There is a minute-long video of a mother wild enough to terrify wolves, a freezing morning, a trap made of invisible wire, a person with exactly the right pair of hands, and a finale that I will think about for a very long time. It is not loud. It is not flashy. It is not trying to go viral.
It just happens to be one of the most human things I have ever seen, and the humans are not even the main characters.
Watch the mother.
Then watch the ending.
23/ ONE LAST THING
The internet is a loud place. Most of what gets attention is built to make you tired.
So when something quiet and true comes along, something that asks nothing from you except sixty seconds and an open heart, it feels almost like a small rebellion to give it your attention.
Give it your attention.
Then give a little of that attention to the world around you. To the fence on your road. To the animal in the ditch. To the person at the edge of the room who looks like they could use a hand.
Most of the good that happens on this planet does not make headlines. It happens in the cold, at dawn, between two living things who have no reason to trust each other, and decide to anyway.
That is the whole story.
It is also the whole point.
If this hit you the way it hit me, repost it. Not for me. For the next person who needs a minute of proof that the world still has this in it.
And if you only do one thing today:
Watch the mother.
P.S. If you already watched it, you know. If you have not, you are about to lose sixty seconds and gain a story you will tell for years. Press play before the feeling fades.

3）
was not merely a measure for "freeze protection," but rather the removal of federally mandated emission control devices, coupled with the concealment of these actions from diagnostic systems. Such practices are not uncommon within the diesel-modification subculture—driven by a desire for more horsepower, a wish to avoid high repair costs, or even the "rolling coal" trend. During the Biden administration, the EPA and the Department of Justice have intensified criminal enforcement against the use of "defeat devices."
A deeper, systemic analysis:
This situation exposes the conflict between one-size-fits-all federal regulation and the extreme realities faced on the ground. Emission standards drafted in Washington offices are based on assumptions of average or temperate climates, failing to account for the engineering and survival challenges unique to Alaska (and other northern regions). Diesel vehicles serve as the lifeline for heavy transport, logistics, and resource industries in Alaska. When emission-control systems become a "safety risk," mechanics opting to "delete" or modify them is a market response to regulatory failure. The bureaucracy prioritizes emission-reduction figures and compliance records on paper, rather than the safety of drivers who might otherwise freeze to death in their vehicles on the road. The deployment of 30 armed agents to raid a small repair shop—especially when weighed against transnational crime, border issues, or other pressing law-enforcement priorities—highlights a clear misallocation of resources and creates the impression of "performative enforcement."
At the same time, environmental regulations do not exist in a vacuum; nitrogen oxides (NOx) and particulate matter from diesel exhaust do indeed impact air quality and public health. The issue lies in the method of enforcement: criminalizing the modifications that mechanics make to ensure operational viability, rather than prioritizing technological improvements (such as emission systems better adapted for extreme cold), regional exemptions, or practical, feasible alternatives. Alaskans, including Senator Dan Sullivan, have long criticized "Obama-era diesel emission rules" as being entirely unrealistic for cold-weather regions. The Trump administration later adjusted enforcement priorities and granted pardons in several similar cases.
On a political and cultural level, this has become a textbook example for the "Green New Deal" (or "Green New Scam") narrative—even though the legal basis is the Clean Air Act rather than specific "Green New Deal" legislation. It reinforces the dichotomy between "Washington elites" and "working-class laborers"—pitting metrics devised in climate-controlled offices against the harsh realities of survival in a frozen wilderness. In July 2026, following an appeal by Sullivan, Trump granted a full, unconditional pardon to Spurlock. On October 13, at a rally in Wasilla, he also issued on-the-spot pardons to two other individuals—Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming, associated with "Arm Rippin Toys"—who, like Spurlock, were diesel mechanics. Citing Spurlock’s case, Trump publicly criticized the Biden administration for "targeting the Alaskan way of life." This move served both to mobilize his grassroots base and to offer a political response to regulatory overreach.
Viewed from a broader perspective, this reflects the inherent tensions within U.S. environmental policy: the push for idealized, uniform national standards versus the reality of geographic, climatic, and economic diversity; the use of criminal enforcement for routine commercial activities rather than civil or administrative remedies; and the conflict between the expansion of federal power and the autonomy of states and localities. For a state like Alaska, issues surrounding energy, transportation, and extreme environmental conditions are matters of survival, not abstract environmental dogma. Trump’s pardons and public backing transformed these

text:
President Trump said on October 13 that he did not believe Russia was helping Iran. This raises a question: is this information really being withheld from the US president?

In 2025, Russia and Iran signed a 20-year strategic treaty. They help each other with weapons, technology, and money to sustain their wars and weaken the United States.

Iran attacks shipping to keep oil prices high. According to Reuters on October 14, 2026, two senior Iranian officials directly linked this strategy to the US elections on November 3. They also discussed expanding attacks beyond the Strait of Hormuz. This benefits Russia: its oil becomes more expensive, buyers accept smaller discounts, and demand rises. According to CREA, high prices helped Moscow maintain its revenues at the end of March, even after Ukrainian strikes on Russian export infrastructure.

Russia offers the US its diesel and gets sanctions relief. Iran disrupts fuel supplies, while Moscow offers to help and receives concessions in return.

Iran gave Russia Shahed-131/136 drones, components, equipment, and technology to manufacture drones in Alabuga. Russia is now returning the favor by supplying Iran with improved drones and sharing its experience in bypassing air defense systems. On March 27, 2026, the Associated Press, citing US and European officials, reported deliveries of such drones to Iran. Additional reports about Russian components and their use emerged in August. Iran provided the original technology; Russia refined it in Ukraine, and those improvements are now helping Iran attack US forces.

Russia provides Iran with intelligence on US facilities. In September, CNN linked Russian satellite intelligence to Iran’s March 27 attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. The strike wounded 12 US service members and destroyed an AWACS aircraft.

Russia is helping Iran develop engines for supersonic cruise missiles. On September 1, 2026, the Financial Times reported on a secret program known as C430L, which has been operating since 2023. Russian specialists linked to Rosoboronexport and the United Shipbuilding Corporation’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya are involved. The program could allow Iran to manufacture more sophisticated weapons capable of threatening US ships and bases in the region.

Iran supplies Russia with ballistic missiles and trains Russian troops to use them. In September 2024, the US officially announced the first delivery of Fath-360 missiles and reported that Iranian instructors were training Russian missile crews. For Moscow, this means additional ammunition for its war against Ukraine.

Russia sells Iran air defense systems and combat aircraft. In February 2026, the Financial Times reported a contract worth approximately €495 million for 500 Verba man-portable air defense launchers and 2,500 missiles, scheduled for delivery between 2027 and 2029. Iran has also confirmed purchasing Su-35 fighter jets, while visual evidence of the first Mi-28 helicopter deliveries emerged in January 2026. The exact number of aircraft and helicopters Iran has received remains unclear.

Russia is transferring US weapons captured in Ukraine to Iran. In March 2023, CNN reported that Russia had handed over Javelin and Stinger. US sources expected Iran to attempt to dismantle and copy the systems. Even if reverse-engineering fails, Tehran can study how they work and how to counter them.

Russia helps the Houthis through Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). According to the Wall Street Journal in October 2024, the Houthis received Russian satellite data through this channel to target commercial shipping. Reuters also reported that Iran had acted as an intermediary in talks over possible Russian deliveries of Yakhont anti-ship missiles. It has not been established whether those deliveries took place.

Iranian allies attack maritime routes and facilities belonging to US partners. Following an attack on Aramco’s headquarters, the Houthis vowed on October 14 to continue strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities. The US and its allies are consequently forced to defend more sites and commit additional resources.

Russia’s VTB bank helps Iranian banks process payments in circumvention of sanctions. On September 14, 2026, the US Treasury Department sanctioned VTB over its dealings with sanctioned Iranian banks, settlements in rubles and rials, and attempts to move billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets.

This gives Tehran access to funds that Washington had sought to block.

The Russia-linked A7 network helps Iran receive oil revenues and pay for weapons. According to documents released by the US Treasury Department and FinCEN on October 1, its intermediaries also worked with Iran’s central bank and the IRGC. One intermediary and an affiliated company received nearly $140 million from entities involved in evading Iranian sanctions. Financial schemes developed for Russia are also serving Iran’s needs.

Russia and Iran transport weapons in both directions across the Caspian Sea. The US Treasury Department identified the vessel Port Olya-3 as having transported Iranian missiles to Russia. In August 2026, NBC, citing a European government document, reported Russian shipments of drone components, ammunition, and explosives to the Iranian port of Amirabad. This route allows the two countries to supply each other directly with military cargo.

Russia and Iran are developing the International North–South Transport Corridor together with India. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the project accelerated after 2022, partly to reduce dependence on Western routes and exposure to sanctions enforcement.

Russia supports Iran’s nuclear energy sector and is preparing gas projects. Moscow helps operate the Bushehr nuclear power plant and build additional reactor units. Following wartime evacuations, Russian engineers began returning in August 2026. The two countries are also discussing gas supplies of up to 55 billion cubic meters annually, although this remains a proposed volume.

Russia launches Iranian satellites. In July 2025, Russia launched Iran’s Nahid-2 telecommunications satellite into orbit.

Russia and Iran exchange technologies for internet surveillance and communications interception. This cooperation is underpinned by a 2021 agreement and the 2025 strategic treaty. CSIS has also documented Russian assistance to Iran in intercepting telecommunications.

Russia and Iran conduct influence operations targeting US elections. The US Treasury Department documented campaigns by both countries during the 2024 elections.

Russia shields Iran from international scrutiny. On September 17, 2026, Russia and China blocked the extension of the mandate of a UN expert panel monitoring compliance with sanctions against Tehran. This makes it more difficult to independently document violations and increase pressure on Iran.

February 2014: Russian forces seize Crimea.

March 2014: Russia illegally annexes Crimea.
